📓 Python Programming - File Handling 1. Text File Operations Python provides easy ways to handle files for reading and writing. Common File Modes: - 'r' → Read (default) 'w' → Write (overwrites existing file or creates new) 'a' → Append (adds to existing file) 'rb' / 'wb' → Read/Write binary files ➤ Reading a Text File: # Writing sample content for demonstration with open ( "../files/sample.txt" , "w" ) as file : file . write ( "Hello, this is a text file. 
 Second line of text." ) # Reading file with open ( "../files/sample.txt" , "r" ) as file : content = file . read () print ( content ) ➤ Writing to a Text File: with open ( "../files/output.txt" , "w" ) as file : file . write ( "This is a new file. 
 File handling in Python is easy!" ) ➤ Reading Files Line by Line: # Method 1: Using readlines() with open ( "../files/sample.txt" , "r" ) as file : lines = file . readlines () for i , line in enumerate ( lines , 1 ): print ( f "Line { i } : { line . strip () } " ) print ( " 
 " + "=" * 30 + " 
 " ) # Method 2: Using for loop (memory efficient) with open ( "../files/sample.txt" , "r" ) as file : for line_num , line in enumerate ( file , 1 ): print ( f "Line { line_num } : { line . strip () } " ) print ( " 
 " + "=" * 30 + " 
 " ) # Method 3: Using readline() - one line at a time with open ( "../files/sample.txt" , "r" ) as file : line = file . readline () while line : print ( f "Read: { line . strip () } " ) line = file . readline () ➤ Error Handling in File Operations: # Handling FileNotFoundError try : with open ( "../files/nonexistent.txt" , "r" ) as file : content = file . read () print ( content ) except FileNotFoundError : print ( "Error: File not found!" ) except PermissionError : print ( "Error: Permission denied!" ) except Exception as e : print ( f "Unexpected error: { e } " ) # Safe file writing with error handling def safe_write_file ( filename , content ): try : with open ( filename , "w" ) as file : file . write ( content ) print ( f "Successfully wrote to { filename } " ) except PermissionError : print ( f "Error: No permission to write to { filename } " ) except Exception as e : print ( f "Error writing file: { e } " ) # Test the function safe_write_file ( "../files/test_write.txt" , "Hello, World!" ) # Safe file reading function def safe_read_file ( filename ): try : with open ( filename , "r" ) as file : return file . read () except FileNotFoundError : return f "Error: File ' { filename } ' not found" except PermissionError : return f "Error: No permission to read ' { filename } '" except Exception as e : return f "Error reading file: { e } " # Test the function content = safe_read_file ( "../files/test_write.txt" ) print ( content ) 2. File Path Handling with os Module The os module helps work with file paths in a platform-independent way. import os # Current working directory print ( "Current Directory:" , os . getcwd ()) # Create a file path file_path = os . path . join ( os . getcwd (), "output.txt" ) print ( "File Path:" , file_path ) ➤ Checking File Existence & Operations: # Check if file exists if os . path . exists ( "../files/sample.txt" ): print ( "File exists!" ) else : print ( "File does not exist." ) # Get file size if os . path . exists ( "../files/sample.txt" ): file_size = os . path . getsize ( "../files/sample.txt" ) print ( f "File size: { file_size } bytes" ) # List files in directory files = os . listdir ( "../files/" ) print ( "Files in directory:" , files ) # Create directory if it doesn't exist if not os . path . exists ( "../files/new_folder" ): os . makedirs ( "../files/new_folder" ) print ( "Directory created!" ) else : print ( "Directory already exists!" ) 3. Working with CSV Files CSV (Comma-Separated Values): - Simple format for storing tabular data. Python provides the csv module to work with CSV files. ➤ Reading a CSV File: import csv # Creating a sample CSV file with open ( "../files/data.csv" , "w" , newline = "" ) as file : writer = csv . writer ( file ) writer . writerow ([ "Name" , "Age" ]) writer . writerow ([ "Alice" , 23 ]) writer . writerow ([ "Bob" , 28 ]) # Reading the CSV file with open ( "../files/data.csv" , "r" ) as file : reader = csv . reader ( file ) for row in reader : print ( row ) ➤ Using Dictionaries in CSV Files: # Writing using DictWriter with open ( "../files/data_dict.csv" , "w" , newline = "" ) as file : fieldnames = [ "Name" , "Age" ] writer = csv . DictWriter ( file , fieldnames = fieldnames ) writer . writeheader () writer . writerow ({ "Name" : "Charlie" , "Age" : 30 }) writer . writerow ({ "Name" : "Dana" , "Age" : 26 }) # Reading using DictReader with open ( "../files/data_dict.csv" , "r" ) as file : reader = csv . DictReader ( file ) for row in reader : print ( row ) 4. Working with JSON JSON (JavaScript Object Notation): - Popular data format for exchanging data. Similar to Python dictionaries. ➤ Reading & Writing JSON: import json # Python dictionary person = { "name" : "Eve" , "age" : 29 , "skills" : [ "Python" , "Data Science" ]} # Writing to JSON file with open ( "../files/person.json" , "w" ) as file : json . dump ( person , file ) # Reading JSON file with open ( "../files/person.json" , "r" ) as file : data = json . load ( file ) print ( data ) ➤ Parsing JSON Strings: # JSON string json_str = '{"name": "Frank", "age": 32}' # Converting JSON string to dictionary person = json . loads ( json_str ) print ( person [ "name" ]) 5. Binary File Handling Binary files store data in binary format (images, videos, executables, etc.) ➤ Reading & Writing Binary Files: # Write binary data binary_data = b "Hello, this is binary data! \x00\x01\x02 " with open ( "../files/binary_file.bin" , "wb" ) as file : file . write ( binary_data ) # Read binary data with open ( "../files/binary_file.bin" , "rb" ) as file : data = file . read () print ( f "Binary data: { data } " ) print ( f "Data type: { type ( data ) } " ) # Copy a file using binary mode (useful for images, videos, etc.) def copy_file ( source , destination ): try : with open ( source , "rb" ) as src : with open ( destination , "wb" ) as dst : dst . write ( src . read ()) print ( f "File copied from { source } to { destination } " ) except FileNotFoundError : print ( f "Source file { source } not found" ) except Exception as e : print ( f "Error copying file: { e } " ) # Create a test file and copy it with open ( "../files/test_source.txt" , "w" ) as file : file . write ( "This is a test file to copy." ) copy_file ( "../files/test_source.txt" , "../files/test_copy.txt" ) 6. Modern File Handling with pathlib pathlib is a modern, object-oriented way to handle file paths (Python 3.4+) ➤ Using pathlib for File Operations: from pathlib import Path # Create Path objects current_dir = Path . cwd () print ( f "Current directory: { current_dir } " ) # Create file path file_path = Path ( "../files/pathlib_test.txt" ) print ( f "File path: { file_path } " ) # Check if file exists print ( f "File exists: { file_path . exists () } " ) # Create parent directories if they don't exist file_path . parent . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) # Write to file using pathlib file_path . write_text ( "Hello from pathlib!" ) # Read from file using pathlib content = file_path . read_text () print ( f "File content: { content } " ) # Get file information if file_path . exists (): print ( f "File size: { file_path . stat () . st_size } bytes" ) print ( f "File name: { file_path . name } " ) print ( f "File extension: { file_path . suffix } " ) print ( f "Parent directory: { file_path . parent } " ) # List files in directory files_dir = Path ( "../files" ) if files_dir . exists (): print ( " 
 Files in directory:" ) for file in files_dir . iterdir (): if file . is_file (): print ( f " 📄 { file . name } " ) elif file . is_dir (): print ( f " 📁 { file . name } /" ) # Find files by pattern print ( " 
 Text files:" ) for txt_file in files_dir . glob ( "*.txt" ): print ( f " 📄 { txt_file . name } " ) # Working with different path parts sample_path = Path ( "/home/user/documents/file.txt" ) print ( f " 
 Path parts:" ) print ( f " Root: { sample_path . root } " ) print ( f " Parts: { sample_path . parts } " ) print ( f " Parent: { sample_path . parent } " ) print ( f " Name: { sample_path . name } " ) print ( f " Stem: { sample_path . stem } " ) print ( f " Suffix: { sample_path . suffix } " ) 7. Practical File Handling Examples ➤ Log File Processing: # Create a sample log file log_content = """2024-01-15 10:30:25 INFO User logged in 2024-01-15 10:31:15 ERROR Failed to connect to database 2024-01-15 10:32:45 INFO Database connection restored 2024-01-15 10:33:20 WARNING High memory usage detected 2024-01-15 10:34:10 INFO User logged out""" with open ( "../files/app.log" , "w" ) as file : file . write ( log_content ) # Process log file def analyze_log_file ( filename ): log_stats = { "INFO" : 0 , "ERROR" : 0 , "WARNING" : 0 } try : with open ( filename , "r" ) as file : for line in file : if "INFO" in line : log_stats [ "INFO" ] += 1 elif "ERROR" in line : log_stats [ "ERROR" ] += 1 elif "WARNING" in line : log_stats [ "WARNING" ] += 1 return log_stats except FileNotFoundError : return "Log file not found" # Analyze the log stats = analyze_log_file ( "../files/app.log" ) print ( "Log Analysis:" ) for level , count in stats . items (): print ( f " { level } : { count } messages" ) # Filter errors from log def extract_errors ( log_file , error_file ): try : with open ( log_file , "r" ) as infile , open ( error_file , "w" ) as outfile : for line in infile : if "ERROR" in line : outfile . write ( line ) print ( f "Errors extracted to { error_file } " ) except FileNotFoundError : print ( f "Log file { log_file } not found" ) extract_errors ( "../files/app.log" , "../files/errors.log" ) ➤ Configuration File Handling: # Create a configuration file config = { "database" : { "host" : "localhost" , "port" : 5432 , "username" : "admin" }, "app" : { "name" : "MyApp" , "version" : "1.0.0" , "debug" : True } } # Save configuration with open ( "../files/config.json" , "w" ) as file : json . dump ( config , file , indent = 2 ) # Load and use configuration def load_config ( filename ): try : with open ( filename , "r" ) as file : return json . load ( file ) except FileNotFoundError : print ( f "Config file { filename } not found" ) return None except json . JSONDecodeError : print ( f "Invalid JSON in { filename } " ) return None # Load configuration app_config = load_config ( "../files/config.json" ) if app_config : print ( f "App Name: { app_config [ 'app' ][ 'name' ] } " ) print ( f "Database Host: { app_config [ 'database' ][ 'host' ] } " ) print ( f "Debug Mode: { app_config [ 'app' ][ 'debug' ] } " ) # Update configuration def update_config ( filename , section , key , value ): config = load_config ( filename ) if config : config [ section ][ key ] = value with open ( filename , "w" ) as file : json . dump ( config , file , indent = 2 ) print ( f "Updated { section } . { key } = { value } " ) # Update debug mode update_config ( "../files/config.json" , "app" , "debug" , False ) Example Prompt to ChatGPT: ``` "Generate Python code to read a JSON file containing student records and print their names." 🎯 Quick Recap ✅ File operations: reading, writing, appending, line-by-line processing ✅ Error handling: try-except blocks for robust file operations ✅ Use os module for file path handling and file system operations ✅ CSV files: csv.reader , csv.writer , and dictionaries ✅ JSON: Read, write, parse structured data ✅ Binary files: handling images, executables, and other binary data ✅ Modern pathlib : object-oriented file path handling ✅ Practical examples: log processing, configuration files 📝 Practice Exercises Basic Level: Write a program to create a text file with your name and age. Read the file you just created and print its contents. Create a CSV file with three student records (name, age, grade). Read and print all names from the CSV file. Write a program to save a dictionary as a JSON file and read it back. Intermediate Level: Write a program that reads a text file line by line and counts the number of lines. Create a program that handles FileNotFoundError when trying to read a non-existent file. Write a function that copies a file from one location to another using binary mode. Use pathlib to create a directory and list all .txt files in it. Create a log analyzer that counts different log levels (INFO, ERROR, WARNING). Advanced Level: Write a program that reads a large file efficiently without loading it entirely into memory. Create a configuration manager that loads, updates, and saves JSON configuration files. Write a file backup system that creates timestamped backups of important files. Build a CSV data processor that filters and transforms data before saving. Create a file monitor that tracks changes in a directory and logs them.

 " ) # Method 3: Using readline() - one line at a time with open ( "../files/sample.txt" , "r" ) as file : line = file . readline () while line : print ( f "Read: { line . strip () } " ) line = file . readline () ➤ Error Handling in File Operations: # Handling FileNotFoundError try : with open ( "../files/nonexistent.txt" , "r" ) as file : content = file . read () print ( content ) except FileNotFoundError : print ( "Error: File not found!" ) except PermissionError : print ( "Error: Permission denied!" ) except Exception as e : print ( f "Unexpected error: { e } " ) # Safe file writing with error handling def safe_write_file ( filename , content ): try : with open ( filename , "w" ) as file : file . write ( content ) print ( f "Successfully wrote to { filename } " ) except PermissionError : print ( f "Error: No permission to write to { filename } " ) except Exception as e : print ( f "Error writing file: { e } " ) # Test the function safe_write_file ( "../files/test_write.txt" , "Hello, World!" ) # Safe file reading function def safe_read_file ( filename ): try : with open ( filename , "r" ) as file : return file . read () except FileNotFoundError : return f "Error: File ' { filename } ' not found" except PermissionError : return f "Error: No permission to read ' { filename } '" except Exception as e : return f "Error reading file: { e } " # Test the function content = safe_read_file ( "../files/test_write.txt" ) print ( content )

docs.text: 📓 Python Programming - Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) 1. Classes & Objects What is OOP? Organizes code around real-world entities (objects). Class : Blueprint for creating objects. Object : An instance of a class. # Defining a class class Student : pass # Creating an object s1 = Student () print ( type ( s1 )) 2. Class vs Object Attributes Class attributes : Shared by all objects. Object attributes : Unique to each object. ➤ Example: class Student : college = "Westcliff University" # Class attribute def __init__ ( self , name , age ): self . name = name # Object attribute self . age = age s1 = Student ( "Alice" , 20 ) s2 = Student ( "Bob" , 22 ) print ( s1 . name , s1 . college ) print ( s2 . name , s2 . college ) 3. Initializing Object Attributes with __init__() __init__() is a special method that runs when an object is created. (Like Constructor) ➤ Example: class Car : def __init__ ( self , brand , year ): self . brand = brand self . year = year c1 = Car ( "Toyota" , 2020 ) print ( c1 . brand , c1 . year ) 4. The self Keyword Refers to the current object. Used to access object attributes and methods. ➤ Example: class Dog : def __init__ ( self , name ): self . name = name def speak ( self ): print ( f " { self . name } says Woof!" ) d = Dog ( "Buddy" ) d . speak () 5. Inheritance Inheritance allows a class to use properties and methods of another class. Types: - Single Inheritance Multiple Inheritance Multi-Level Inheritance ➤ Single Inheritance: class Animal : def speak ( self ): print ( "Animal sound" ) class Dog ( Animal ): def bark ( self ): print ( "Woof!" ) d = Dog () d . speak () d . bark () ➤ Multiple Inheritance: class A : def show_a ( self ): print ( "A" ) class B : def show_b ( self ): print ( "B" ) class C ( A , B ): pass c = C () c . show_a () c . show_b () ➤ Multi-Level Inheritance: class Grandparent : def grandparent_func ( self ): print ( "Grandparent" ) class Parent ( Grandparent ): def parent_func ( self ): print ( "Parent" ) class Child ( Parent ): def child_func ( self ): print ( "Child" ) c = Child () c . grandparent_func () c . parent_func () c . child_func () 6. Polymorphism & Operator Overloading Polymorphism: Same function name but different behaviors. Operator Overloading: Using special methods to define how operators behave for custom objects. ➤ Polymorphism Example: class Cat : def sound ( self ): print ( "Meow" ) class Dog : def sound ( self ): print ( "Woof" ) animals = [ Cat (), Dog ()] for animal in animals : animal . sound () Traditional Overloading Does Not Work in Python def greet ( name ): print ( f "Hello, { name } !" ) def greet ( name , age ): print ( f "Hello, { name } ! You are { age } years old." ) greet ( "Alice" ) # ❌ TypeError: greet() missing 1 required positional argument: 'age' ➤ Python's Way of Function Overloading: Python does not support function overloading in the traditional sense, as seen in languages like C++ or Java. In those languages, you can have multiple functions with the same name but different parameters (type or number). Python, however, allows you to define a function only once. If you define it again, it simply overwrites the previous definition. But there is some work around this. Discuss how to implement function overloading in Python using default arguments or variable-length arguments. # Using default arguments for overloading-like behavior def greet ( name , age = None ): if age is None : print ( f "Hello, { name } !" ) else : print ( f "Hello, { name } ! You are { age } years old." ) greet ( "Alice" ) # Works! greet ( "Bob" , 25 ) # Also works! # Using *args for variable arguments def add ( * numbers ): return sum ( numbers ) print ( add ( 1 , 2 )) # 3 print ( add ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 )) # 10 ➤ Operator Overloading Example: class Point : def __init__ ( self , x ): self . x = x def __add__ ( self , other ): return Point ( self . x + other . x ) p1 = Point ( 5 ) p2 = Point ( 10 ) result = p1 + p2 print ( result . x ) 7. Function Overriding & Encapsulation Function Overriding: Child class redefines a method from the parent class. Encapsulation: Restricts direct access to variables using private/protected attributes. ➤ Function Overriding Example: class Animal : def speak ( self ): print ( "Animal sound" ) class Dog ( Animal ): def speak ( self ): print ( "Woof!" ) d = Dog () d . speak () ➤ Encapsulation Example: class BankAccount : def __init__ ( self , balance ): self . __balance = balance # Private attribute def get_balance ( self ): return self . __balance def deposit ( self , amount ): self . __balance += amount acc = BankAccount ( 1000 ) acc . deposit ( 500 ) print ( acc . get_balance ()) ➤ Using Properties (Getters & Setters): class Temperature : def __init__ ( self ): self . _celsius = 0 @property def celsius ( self ): return self . _celsius @celsius . setter def celsius ( self , value ): if value < - 273.15 : raise ValueError ( "Temperature below absolute zero is not possible" ) self . _celsius = value @property def fahrenheit ( self ): return ( self . _celsius * 9 / 5 ) + 32 # Usage temp = Temperature () temp . celsius = 25 print ( f "Celsius: { temp . celsius } " ) print ( f "Fahrenheit: { temp . fahrenheit } " ) 8. Class Methods & Static Methods Class Methods & Static Methods: Instance Method : Needs self , works with object data Class Method : Uses @classmethod , gets cls parameter Static Method : Uses @staticmethod , independent function inside class ➤ Example: class Person : species = "Homo sapiens" # Class attribute def __init__ ( self , name , age ): self . name = name # Instance attribute self . age = age # Instance method def introduce ( self ): return f "Hi, I'm { self . name } , { self . age } years old" # Class method @classmethod def get_species ( cls ): return cls . species @classmethod def create_baby ( cls , name ): return cls ( name , 0 ) # Alternative constructor # Static method @staticmethod def is_adult ( age ): return age >= 18 # Usage examples p1 = Person ( "Alice" , 25 ) print ( p1 . introduce ()) # Instance method print ( Person . get_species ()) # Class method baby = Person . create_baby ( "Bob" ) # Class method as constructor print ( baby . introduce ()) print ( Person . is_adult ( 17 )) # Static method print ( Person . is_adult ( 20 )) 9. Special Methods (Magic Methods) Special methods start and end with double underscores __ Common ones: - __str__() → What users see when printing - __repr__() → Developer representation - __len__() → Makes objects work with len() - __eq__() → Custom equality comparison ➤ Example: class Book : def __init__ ( self , title , pages ): self . title = title self . pages = pages def __str__ ( self ): return f "Book: { self . title } " def __repr__ ( self ): return f "Book(' { self . title } ', { self . pages } )" def __len__ ( self ): return self . pages def __eq__ ( self , other ): return self . title == other . title # Testing special methods book1 = Book ( "Python Guide" , 300 ) book2 = Book ( "Python Guide" , 350 ) print ( book1 ) # Uses __str__ print ( repr ( book1 )) # Uses __repr__ print ( len ( book1 )) # Uses __len__ print ( book1 == book2 ) # Uses __eq__ # Create a list of books books = [ book1 , Book ( "Java Guide" , 400 )] print ( f "Total pages: { sum ( len ( book ) for book in books ) } " ) 10. Composition vs Inheritance Two ways to reuse code: Inheritance : "IS-A" relationship (Dog IS-A Animal) Composition : "HAS-A" relationship (Car HAS-A Engine) ➤ Composition Example: # Composition example class Engine : def __init__ ( self , horsepower ): self . horsepower = horsepower def start ( self ): return f "Engine with { self . horsepower } hp started!" class Car : def __init__ ( self , brand , engine ): self . brand = brand self . engine = engine # Car HAS-A Engine def start_car ( self ): return f " { self . brand } : { self . engine . start () } " # Usage engine = Engine ( 200 ) car = Car ( "Toyota" , engine ) print ( car . start_car ()) # Compare with inheritance approach class Animal : def breathe ( self ): return "Breathing..." class Dog ( Animal ): # Dog IS-A Animal def bark ( self ): return "Woof!" dog = Dog () print ( dog . breathe ()) # Inherited method print ( dog . bark ()) # Own method 🎯 Quick Recap ✅ OOP models real-world entities with classes and objects ✅ Class attributes shared, object attributes unique ✅ Inheritance promotes code reuse (IS-A relationship) ✅ Composition provides flexibility (HAS-A relationship) ✅ Polymorphism enables flexibility through method overriding ✅ Properties provide clean encapsulation with getters/setters ✅ Class methods and static methods offer different functionality levels ✅ Special methods make objects work with built-in functions ✅ Function overriding & encapsulation provide safety and control 📝 Practice Exercises Basic Level: Create a Car class with brand and year, and display details using a method. Demonstrate single inheritance with Animal → Bird . Create a class Rectangle that overloads + to add areas of two rectangles. Use encapsulation to hide a bank account's balance and provide methods to deposit/withdraw. Demonstrate function overriding using a parent-child class structure. Intermediate Level: Create a Person class with properties for name and age validation. Build a Calculator class with static methods for basic operations. Create a Book class with special methods ( __str__ , __len__ , __eq__ ). Use composition to create a Computer class that HAS-A Processor . Create a class method that works as an alternative constructor. Advanced Level: Build a complete BankAccount system with properties and validation. Create a polymorphic system with different Shape classes. Implement a Library class that manages Book objects using composition. Design a class hierarchy for different types of vehicles with proper inheritance. Create a Temperature class with property decorators for Celsius/Fahrenheit conversion.

docs.text: Two ways to reuse code: Inheritance : "IS-A" relationship (Dog IS-A Animal) Composition : "HAS-A" relationship (Car HAS-A Engine) ➤ Composition Example: # Composition example class Engine : def __init__ ( self , horsepower ): self . horsepower = horsepower def start ( self ): return f "Engine with { self . horsepower } hp started!" class Car : def __init__ ( self , brand , engine ): self . brand = brand self . engine = engine # Car HAS-A Engine def start_car ( self ): return f " { self . brand } : { self . engine . start () } " # Usage engine = Engine ( 200 ) car = Car ( "Toyota" , engine ) print ( car . start_car ()) # Compare with inheritance approach class Animal : def breathe ( self ): return "Breathing..." class Dog ( Animal ): # Dog IS-A Animal def bark ( self ): return "Woof!" dog = Dog () print ( dog . breathe ()) # Inherited method print ( dog . bark ()) # Own method
docs.title: 10. Composition vs Inheritance

docs.text: ✅ OOP models real-world entities with classes and objects ✅ Class attributes shared, object attributes unique ✅ Inheritance promotes code reuse (IS-A relationship) ✅ Composition provides flexibility (HAS-A relationship) ✅ Polymorphism enables flexibility through method overriding ✅ Properties provide clean encapsulation with getters/setters ✅ Class methods and static methods offer different functionality levels ✅ Special methods make objects work with built-in functions ✅ Function overriding & encapsulation provide safety and control

📓 Python Programming - Error Handling and Debugging 1. Try-Except Blocks Error handling prevents programs from crashing due to unexpected issues. The basic structure: try : # Code that might raise an error except : # Code to handle the error ➤ ** Example : ** ``` python try : num = int ( input ( "Enter a number: " )) print ( f "Square: { num ** 2 } " ) except Exception as e : print ( "Invalid input! Please enter a number. 
 Exception:" , e ) 2. Catching Specific Exceptions It's better to catch specific exceptions to handle different errors appropriately. try : num = int ( input ( "Enter a number: " )) result = 10 / num except ValueError : print ( "Please enter a valid number." ) except ZeroDivisionError : print ( "Division by zero is not allowed." ) except Exception as e : print ( "An unexpected error occurred:" , e ) 3. Using else & finally else: Runs if no exceptions occur. finally: Runs no matter what (cleanup code). try : num = int ( input ( "Enter a positive number: " )) except ValueError : print ( "Invalid input." ) else : print ( f "You entered: { num } " ) finally : print ( "This always runs." ) 4. Generating and Creating Custom Exceptions You can use raise to generate exceptions. Custom exceptions are created by defining a new class that inherits from Exception . ➤ Raising Exceptions Example: age = - 5 if age < 0 : raise ValueError ( "Age cannot be negative." ) ➤ Custom Exception Example: class NegativeAgeError ( Exception ): pass age = - 5 try : if age < 0 : raise NegativeAgeError ( "Age cannot be negative." ) except NegativeAgeError as e : print ( e ) 5. Problem-Solving Strategies ✅ Understand the error message. ✅ Use print statements or debugging tools to trace the problem. ✅ Break the code into smaller parts. ✅ Handle exceptions gracefully using try-except blocks. ✅ Anticipate common errors (e.g., invalid input, division by zero). ✅ Write custom exceptions for specific situations. 6. Common Python Error Types Understanding common errors helps you debug faster: SyntaxError : Invalid Python syntax NameError : Variable not defined TypeError : Wrong data type used IndexError : List index out of range KeyError : Dictionary key doesn't exist FileNotFoundError : File doesn't exist ImportError : Module can't be imported # Examples of common errors (commented out to avoid actual errors) # 1. SyntaxError # print("Hello World" # Missing closing parenthesis # 2. NameError # print(undefined_variable) # Variable not defined # 3. TypeError # result = "5" + 10 # Can't add string and integer # 4. IndexError # my_list = [1, 2, 3] # print(my_list[5]) # Index 5 doesn't exist # 5. KeyError # my_dict = {"name": "John"} # print(my_dict["age"]) # Key 'age' doesn't exist # 6. FileNotFoundError # with open("nonexistent.txt", "r") as file: # content = file.read() # Let's demonstrate with proper error handling: def demonstrate_errors (): # Handling IndexError try : my_list = [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] print ( my_list [ 5 ]) except IndexError as e : print ( f "IndexError caught: { e } " ) # Handling KeyError try : my_dict = { "name" : "John" } print ( my_dict [ "age" ]) except KeyError as e : print ( f "KeyError caught: Missing key { e } " ) # Handling TypeError try : result = "5" + 10 except TypeError as e : print ( f "TypeError caught: { e } " ) demonstrate_errors () 7. Debugging Techniques Different ways to find and fix bugs in your code: Print Debugging : Add print statements to track values Python Debugger (pdb) : Step through code line by line IDE Debugger : Use VS Code's built-in debugger Logging : Better than print statements for production code ➤ Print Debugging Example: def calculate_average ( numbers ): print ( f "DEBUG: Input numbers: { numbers } " ) # Debug print total = 0 for i , num in enumerate ( numbers ): total += num print ( f "DEBUG: Step { i + 1 } , added { num } , total now: { total } " ) # Debug print average = total / len ( numbers ) print ( f "DEBUG: Final average: { average } " ) # Debug print return average # Test with debug prints numbers = [ 10 , 20 , 30 , 40 ] result = calculate_average ( numbers ) print ( f "Average: { result } " ) # Better approach: Use a debug flag DEBUG = True def debug_print ( message ): if DEBUG : print ( f "[DEBUG] { message } " ) def calculate_average_v2 ( numbers ): debug_print ( f "Input numbers: { numbers } " ) total = sum ( numbers ) debug_print ( f "Sum: { total } " ) average = total / len ( numbers ) debug_print ( f "Average: { average } " ) return average print ( " 
 --- Version 2 with debug flag ---" ) result2 = calculate_average_v2 ([ 5 , 15 , 25 ]) print ( f "Average: { result2 } " ) ➤ Using Python's Logging Module: import logging # Configure logging logging . basicConfig ( level = logging . DEBUG , format = ' %(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s ' ) def divide_numbers ( a , b ): logging . debug ( f "Starting division: { a } / { b } " ) try : if b == 0 : logging . error ( "Division by zero attempted!" ) raise ZeroDivisionError ( "Cannot divide by zero" ) result = a / b logging . info ( f "Division successful: { a } / { b } = { result } " ) return result except Exception as e : logging . exception ( "An error occurred during division" ) raise # Test logging print ( "=== Testing with logging ===" ) try : result1 = divide_numbers ( 10 , 2 ) print ( f "Result 1: { result1 } " ) result2 = divide_numbers ( 10 , 0 ) print ( f "Result 2: { result2 } " ) except ZeroDivisionError as e : print ( f "Caught error: { e } " ) # Different log levels logging . debug ( "This is a debug message" ) logging . info ( "This is an info message" ) logging . warning ( "This is a warning message" ) logging . error ( "This is an error message" ) logging . critical ( "This is a critical message" ) 8. Assertions and Testing Assertions help catch bugs early by checking assumptions: assert statement checks if a condition is True Raises AssertionError if condition is False Used for debugging and testing # Basic assertion examples def calculate_factorial ( n ): assert n >= 0 , "Factorial is not defined for negative numbers" assert isinstance ( n , int ), "Input must be an integer" if n == 0 or n == 1 : return 1 result = 1 for i in range ( 2 , n + 1 ): result *= i # Assert the result makes sense assert result > 0 , "Factorial should always be positive" return result # Test assertions try : print ( f "5! = { calculate_factorial ( 5 ) } " ) print ( f "0! = { calculate_factorial ( 0 ) } " ) # This will raise AssertionError print ( f "(-1)! = { calculate_factorial ( - 1 ) } " ) except AssertionError as e : print ( f "Assertion failed: { e } " ) # Assertions in testing def test_factorial (): # Test cases assert calculate_factorial ( 0 ) == 1 , "0! should be 1" assert calculate_factorial ( 1 ) == 1 , "1! should be 1" assert calculate_factorial ( 5 ) == 120 , "5! should be 120" print ( "All factorial tests passed!" ) test_factorial () # Assertions for debugging def divide_positive_numbers ( a , b ): assert a > 0 and b > 0 , "Both numbers must be positive" result = a / b # Check our assumption about the result assert result > 0 , "Result should be positive when dividing positive numbers" return result # Test try : result = divide_positive_numbers ( 10 , 2 ) print ( f "Division result: { result } " ) # This will fail the assertion result = divide_positive_numbers ( - 10 , 2 ) except AssertionError as e : print ( f "Assertion error: { e } " ) 9. Exception Chaining and Context Preserve error context when re-raising exceptions: raise ... from ... - Explicit chaining raise - Implicit chaining Helps track the original cause of errors def read_config_file ( filename ): """Example of exception chaining""" try : with open ( filename , 'r' ) as file : import json config = json . load ( file ) return config except FileNotFoundError as e : # Chain the original exception raise ValueError ( f "Configuration file ' { filename } ' not found" ) from e except json . JSONDecodeError as e : # Chain with more context raise ValueError ( f "Invalid JSON in configuration file ' { filename } '" ) from e def process_data (): """Example showing exception context""" try : config = read_config_file ( "nonexistent_config.json" ) return config except ValueError as e : print ( f "Configuration error: { e } " ) print ( f "Original cause: { e . __cause__ } " ) # Re-raise with additional context raise RuntimeError ( "Failed to initialize application" ) from e # Test exception chaining try : process_data () except RuntimeError as e : print ( f " 
 Final error: { e } " ) print ( f "Caused by: { e . __cause__ } " ) print ( f "Original cause: { e . __cause__ . __cause__ } " ) # Example with suppress chaining def clean_reraise (): try : result = 10 / 0 except ZeroDivisionError : # Suppress the original exception chain raise ValueError ( "Invalid calculation" ) from None try : clean_reraise () except ValueError as e : print ( f " 
 Suppressed chain error: { e } " ) print ( f "Has cause: { e . __cause__ } " ) # Will be None 10. Error Handling Best Practices Guidelines for writing robust, maintainable code: ✅ Be specific : Catch specific exceptions, not generic Exception ✅ Fail fast : Use assertions to catch bugs early ✅ Log errors : Use logging instead of print for production code ✅ Don't ignore : Always handle or log exceptions ✅ Clean up : Use finally or context managers for cleanup ✅ Document : Specify what exceptions your functions can raise ✅ Test : Write tests for both success and failure cases # Example of good error handling practices import logging class DatabaseError ( Exception ): """Custom exception for database operations""" pass class UserNotFoundError ( DatabaseError ): """Raised when user is not found in database""" pass def get_user_by_id ( user_id ): """ Retrieve user by ID from database. Args: user_id (int): The user ID to search for Returns: dict: User information Raises: TypeError: If user_id is not an integer UserNotFoundError: If user is not found DatabaseError: If database connection fails """ # Input validation if not isinstance ( user_id , int ): raise TypeError ( f "user_id must be an integer, got { type ( user_id ) } " ) if user_id <= 0 : raise ValueError ( "user_id must be positive" ) # Simulate database lookup fake_database = { 1 : { "name" : "Alice" , "email" : "alice@example.com" }} try : # Simulate potential database connection error if user_id > 100 : raise ConnectionError ( "Database connection lost" ) if user_id not in fake_database : raise UserNotFoundError ( f "User with ID { user_id } not found" ) user = fake_database [ user_id ] logging . info ( f "Successfully retrieved user { user_id } " ) return user except ConnectionError as e : logging . error ( f "Database connection failed: { e } " ) raise DatabaseError ( "Failed to connect to database" ) from e # Example usage with proper error handling def main (): logging . basicConfig ( level = logging . INFO ) test_cases = [ 1 , "invalid" , - 1 , 2 , 101 ] for user_id in test_cases : try : print ( f " 
 Trying to get user { user_id } :" ) user = get_user_by_id ( user_id ) print ( f "Success: { user } " ) except TypeError as e : print ( f "Type error: { e } " ) except ValueError as e : print ( f "Value error: { e } " ) except UserNotFoundError as e : print ( f "User not found: { e } " ) except DatabaseError as e : print ( f "Database error: { e } " ) print ( f "Original cause: { e . __cause__ } " ) # Run the example main () 🎯 Quick Recap ✅ Use try-except to catch errors and prevent crashes ✅ Catch specific exceptions for better error handling ✅ else and finally provide structured error handling ✅ Custom exceptions allow for clear, descriptive error messages ✅ Know common Python error types for faster debugging ✅ Use debugging techniques: print statements, logging, assertions ✅ Exception chaining preserves error context ✅ Follow best practices for robust, maintainable code ✅ Debugging is an essential skill for reliable code 📝 Practice Exercises Basic Level: Write a program that asks for two numbers and divides them. Handle: ValueError for invalid inputs ZeroDivisionError for division by zero Create a custom exception called PasswordTooShortError if the entered password is less than 8 characters. Demonstrate the use of else and finally in a simple program that reads a file. Intentionally raise an exception if a negative number is entered for age. Intermediate Level: Write a function that catches different types of errors (IndexError, KeyError, TypeError) and prints specific messages for each. Create a simple calculator with proper error handling and logging. Use assertions to validate input in a function that calculates square roots. Write a program that demonstrates exception chaining when processing user data. Advanced Level: Build a file processor that handles multiple types of errors and uses logging instead of print statements. Create a custom exception hierarchy for a banking system (InsufficientFundsError, InvalidAccountError, etc.). Write a robust function with proper documentation that specifies all possible exceptions it can raise. Implement a retry mechanism that attempts an operation multiple times before giving up.

docs.text: 📓 Python Programming - Advanced Python Concepts 1. Lambda Functions (Anonymous Functions) lambda creates small, one-line, anonymous functions. Often used with map() , filter() , sorted() , etc. ➤ Example: # Regular function def square ( x ): return x ** 2 print ( square ( 5 )) # Lambda function square_lambda = lambda x : x ** 2 print ( square_lambda ( 5 )) 2. Generators & Iterators Generators: - Use yield to produce a sequence of values lazily (one at a time). Saves memory compared to lists. Iterators: - Any object with __iter__() and __next__() methods. ➤ Generator Example: def count_up_to ( n ): count = 1 while count <= n : yield count count += 1 print ( count_up_to ( 5 )) # This will print a generator object print ( list ( count_up_to ( 5 ))) for num in count_up_to ( 5 ): print ( num ) ➤ Iterator Example: nums = [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] it = iter ( nums ) print ( next ( it )) print ( next ( it )) print ( next ( it )) 3. List Comprehensions A concise way to create lists in a single line. ➤ Example: # Without list comprehension squares = [] for i in range ( 5 ): squares . append ( i ** 2 ) print ( squares ) # With list comprehension squares = [ i ** 2 for i in range ( 5 )] print ( squares ) # With condition evens = [ i for i in range ( 10 ) if i % 2 == 0 ] print ( evens ) 4. Working with args and *kwargs *args : Allows variable number of positional arguments. **kwargs : Allows variable number of keyword arguments. ➤ Example with *args: def add ( * numbers ): total = sum ( numbers ) print ( "Sum:" , total ) add ( 1 , 2 , 3 ) add ( 4 , 5 ) ➤ Example with **kwargs: def student_info ( ** kwargs ): for key , value in kwargs . items (): print ( f " { key } : { value } " ) student_info ( name = "Alice" , age = 21 , grade = "A" ) ➤ Using map() Function: nums = [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] squared = list ( map ( lambda x : x ** 2 , nums )) print ( squared ) ➤ Using filter() Function: nums = [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] evens = list ( filter ( lambda x : x % 2 == 0 , nums )) print ( evens ) ➤ Using reduce() Function - reduce() applies a function cumulatively to the items of a sequence. It is part of the functools module. from functools import reduce # Multiply all numbers in a list nums = [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] product = reduce ( lambda x , y : x * y , nums ) print ( product ) nums = [ 5 , 10 , 15 ] total_sum = reduce ( lambda x , y : x + y , nums ) print ( total_sum ) ➤ Using enumerate(): fruits = [ "apple" , "banana" , "cherry" ] for index , fruit in enumerate ( fruits , start = 1 ): print ( index , fruit ) 🎯 Quick Recap map() : Apply function to all items filter() : Filter items based on condition reduce() : Cumulatively apply function to reduce a sequence to a single value Lambda: One-line anonymous functions Generators: Produce values lazily with yield Iterators: Objects used to iterate over sequences List comprehensions: Compact way to build lists args, *kwargs: Flexible argument handling 📝 Practice Exercises Write a lambda function to multiply two numbers. Create a generator that yields even numbers from 1 to 10. Use list comprehension to create a list of squares for numbers 1 to 5. Write a function that accepts any number of arguments and prints their sum using *args. Write a function that accepts student details as keyword arguments and prints them. Use map() and filter() to square numbers and filter odd numbers from a list.

Install Homebrew first if needed /bin/bash -c " $( curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh ) " # Install Python brew install python Verify installation: python --version pip --version Git Installation & Setup Install Git 🪟 Windows: Download from https://git-scm.com/download/win and install 🐧 Linux: sudo apt install git 🍎 macOS: brew install git Configure Git git config --global user.name "GithubUsername" git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com" Setup SSH Key # Generate SSH key ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your.email@example.com" # Test connection ssh -T git@github.com Add your SSH key to GitHub: Copy the public key: cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub C:\Users\path.ssh\id_ed25519.pub (For Windows) Go to GitHub Settings → SSH Keys Paste and save VS Code Setup Install VS Code Go to https://code.visualstudio.com/ Download for your operating system Install with default settings Essential Extensions Install these extensions for Python development: Python (Microsoft) Pylance (Microsoft) Python Extension Pack (Microsoft) GitLens (GitKraken) Jupyter (Microsoft) How to install extensions: Open VS Code Click Extensions icon (squares) on left sidebar Search for extension name Click "Install" Virtual Environment Setup Create Virtual Environment # docs.text: Deploying Applications "An application isn't useful until someone can use it." Learning Objectives By the end of this notebook, you will be able to: Explain how HTTP and REST APIs work and how clients consume them Build a REST API with FastAPI backed by a SQLite database Containerise an application using Docker Orchestrate multiple services using Docker Compose Configure Nginx as a reverse proxy in front of a FastAPI application Explain how DNS A records point a domain name to a server IP Prerequisites Python 3.10+ installed Docker Desktop installed and running Basic terminal usage Familiarity with Python functions and classes Install Python dependencies before starting Section 3: pip install fastapi 'uvicorn[standard]' sqlalchemy Section 0 — What We're Building By the end of this notebook, every request made by a browser or curl will travel through this stack: Browser / curl | | HTTP port 80 v [ Nginx ] <-- reverse proxy, handles incoming connections | | HTTP port 8000 (internal Docker network) v [ FastAPI / uvicorn ] <-- application server, runs your Python code | | SQL v [ SQLite ] <-- file-based database, persisted as a Docker volume What Each Layer Does Layer Tool Responsibility Reverse proxy Nginx Accepts public traffic, forwards to the app server Application server FastAPI + uvicorn Handles business logic, validates input, queries DB Database SQLite Stores and retrieves data persistently Container runtime Docker Packages each service so it runs identically everywhere Orchestration Docker Compose Starts all containers with correct wiring in one command The Running Example: Task Manager API We will build a REST API for managing tasks. Every section adds one layer to this same application until the full stack is running. Method Path Action GET /tasks List all tasks POST /tasks Create a new task PATCH /tasks/{id}/complete Mark a task as completed Section 1 — REST APIs & HTTP What Is an API? An API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined way for one program to communicate with another. A web API uses the HTTP protocol — the same protocol your browser uses to load web pages — as the communication channel. When you open https://weather.com , your browser sends an HTTP request and receives an HTML page. When your Python code calls a weather API, it sends the same kind of HTTP request and receives JSON. The protocol is identical; only the response format differs. What Is REST? REST (Representational State Transfer) is a set of conventions for designing web APIs: Resources are identified by URLs ( /tasks , /tasks/42 ) The HTTP method expresses what action to take Responses use standard status codes to communicate the outcome Data is exchanged as JSON An API that follows these conventions is called RESTful . HTTP Methods Method Meaning Typical use GET Retrieve a resource List tasks, get one task POST Create a new resource Add a task PUT Replace a resource entirely Replace all task fields PATCH Update part of a resource Mark a task complete DELETE Remove a resource Delete a task HTTP Status Codes Code Meaning When it happens 200 OK Success GET returned data 201 Created Resource created POST succeeded 204 No Content Success, no response body DELETE succeeded 400 Bad Request Client sent invalid data Missing required field 404 Not Found Resource doesn't exist Task ID not in database 422 Unprocessable Entity Validation failed Wrong data type in body 500 Internal Server Error Server crashed Bug in your code Rule of thumb: 2xx = success, 4xx = the client's fault, 5xx = the server's fault. Anatomy of an HTTP Request and Response REQUEST -------- POST /tasks HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8000 Content-Type: application/json {"title": "Buy groceries"} RESPONSE -------- HTTP/1.1 201 Created Content-Type: application/json {"id": 1, "title": "Buy groceries", "completed": false, "created_at": "2026-04-16T10:00:00"} Every HTTP interaction follows this shape: method + URL + headers + optional body going out, status code + headers + optional body coming back. Section 2 — Browser Clients & Consuming APIs What Is a Client? A client is anything that sends HTTP requests to an API. The API doesn't know or care what type of client is calling it — it only sees an HTTP request. Client Typical use Web browser (via JavaScript) Loads a web app; fetch() calls the API curl Terminal tool for testing APIs manually Postman GUI tool for building and testing requests Python requests / httpx API calls from scripts and services Mobile app iOS/Android apps calling a backend Another server Microservices calling each other How a Browser Consumes an API When a web page needs data, JavaScript uses the fetch API: // JavaScript running in the browser const response = await fetch ( 'http://localhost:8000/tasks' ); const tasks = await response . json (); console . log ( tasks ); // [{"id": 1, "title": "Buy groceries", "completed": false, ...}] The browser sends an HTTP GET to your FastAPI server and receives JSON. Your Python code never knows whether the caller is a browser, a mobile app, or curl . Testing with curl curl is the fastest way to test an API from the terminal: # List all tasks curl http://localhost:8000/tasks # Create a new task curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Buy groceries"}' # Mark task 1 as completed curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/tasks/1/complete FastAPI's Built-in Client: Swagger UI FastAPI automatically generates interactive API documentation at /docs . You can send real HTTP requests directly from the browser — no curl or Postman required. Once you start the server in Section 3, visit: http://localhost:8000/docs Section 3 — FastAPI: First Endpoint What Is FastAPI? FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for building APIs. Key properties: Automatic validation — uses Python type hints and Pydantic to validate all incoming data; returns a 422 with a clear message if the data is wrong Auto-generated docs — Swagger UI at /docs with zero extra code Dependency injection — clean way to share database sessions, auth, and other resources across routes Fast — one of the fastest Python frameworks, powered by Starlette and uvicorn Project Structure Create this directory structure: taskapi/ ├── app/ │ └── main.py └── requirements.txt Version 1: In-Memory Task List Copy the code below into taskapi/app/main.py . This version stores tasks in a Python list. There is no database yet — restart the server and all tasks disappear. Section 4 fixes this. # taskapi/app/main.py (version 1 — in-memory storage) from fastapi import FastAPI , HTTPException from pydantic import BaseModel from datetime import datetime , timezone app = FastAPI ( title = 'Task Manager API' ) # In-memory storage — replaced with SQLite in Section 4 tasks = [] _next_id = 1 class TaskCreate ( BaseModel ): title : str class TaskResponse ( BaseModel ): id : int title : str completed : bool created_at : str @app . get ( '/tasks' , response_model = list [ TaskResponse ]) def list_tasks (): return tasks @app . post ( '/tasks' , response_model = TaskResponse , status_code = 201 ) def create_task ( task : TaskCreate ): global _next_id new_task = { 'id' : _next_id , 'title' : task . title , 'completed' : False , 'created_at' : datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) . isoformat (), } tasks . append ( new_task ) _next_id += 1 return new_task @app . patch ( '/tasks/ {task_id} /complete' , response_model = TaskResponse ) def complete_task ( task_id : int ): for task in tasks : if task [ 'id' ] == task_id : task [ 'completed' ] = True return task raise HTTPException ( status_code = 404 , detail = 'Task not found' ) Running the Application From the taskapi/ directory: uvicorn app.main:app --reload --reload restarts the server automatically when you save a file. Visit: http://localhost:8000/tasks — the raw JSON endpoint http://localhost:8000/docs — Swagger UI (try the endpoints interactively) Testing with curl # Create two tasks curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Buy groceries"}' curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Write tests"}' # List all tasks curl http://localhost:8000/tasks # Complete task 1 curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/tasks/1/complete How FastAPI Handles Validation Send a bad request — omit the required title field: curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{}' FastAPI returns 422 Unprocessable Entity with a detailed error — no extra validation code needed: { "detail" : [{ "loc" : [ "body" , "title" ], "msg" : "field required" , "type" : "value_error.missing" }] } Note: Restart the server and all tasks are gone — the list lives only in memory. Section 4 adds a real database. Section 4 — SQLite Database What Is SQLite? SQLite is a file-based SQL database. The entire database is a single .db file — no separate server process, no configuration. Property SQLite Storage One file ( tasks.db ) Setup None — works out of the box Suitable for Development, small-to-medium production apps, embedded systems Not suitable for High-concurrency write-heavy workloads SQLite is the right choice for this course project and for most applications that do not need horizontal scaling. SQLAlchemy SQLAlchemy is Python's most widely used ORM (Object-Relational Mapper). It lets you define database tables as Python classes and write queries in Python rather than raw SQL. Python class ──────────► database table class Task maps to CREATE TABLE tasks (...) Python object ──────────► database row task = Task(...) maps to INSERT INTO tasks ... Updated Project Structure Add database.py alongside main.py : taskapi/ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py <-- updated (connects to database) │ └── database.py <-- new (engine, session, ORM model) └── requirements.txt Copy database.py below into taskapi/app/database.py : # taskapi/app/database.py import os from sqlalchemy import create_engine , Column , Integer , String , Boolean , DateTime from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker from datetime import datetime DATABASE_URL = os . getenv ( 'DATABASE_URL' , 'sqlite:///./tasks.db' ) engine = create_engine ( DATABASE_URL , connect_args = { 'check_same_thread' : False }) SessionLocal = sessionmaker ( autocommit = False , autoflush = False , bind = engine ) Base = declarative_base () class Task ( Base ): __tablename__ = 'tasks' id = Column ( Integer , primary_key = True , index = True ) title = Column ( String , nullable = False ) completed = Column ( Boolean , default = False ) created_at = Column ( DateTime , default = datetime . utcnow ) def get_db (): """Yield a database session; close it when the request is done.""" db = SessionLocal () try : yield db finally : db . close () def create_tables (): """Create all tables if they do not already exist.""" Base . metadata . create_all ( bind = engine ) Now replace taskapi/app/main.py with the version below. The three routes are identical — only the storage layer changes from a Python list to SQLAlchemy queries. # taskapi/app/main.py (version 2 — SQLite backend) from fastapi import FastAPI , HTTPException , Depends from pydantic import BaseModel from sqlalchemy.orm import Session from app.database import Task , get_db , create_tables app = FastAPI ( title = 'Task Manager API' ) create_tables () # creates tasks.db and the tasks table on first run class TaskCreate ( BaseModel ): title : str class TaskResponse ( BaseModel ): id : int title : str completed : bool created_at : str def _task_to_dict ( task : Task ) -> dict : return { 'id' : task . id , 'title' : task . title , 'completed' : task . completed , 'created_at' : task . created_at . isoformat (), } @app . get ( '/tasks' , response_model = list [ TaskResponse ]) def list_tasks ( db : Session = Depends ( get_db )): return [ _task_to_dict ( t ) for t in db . query ( Task ) . all ()] @app . post ( '/tasks' , response_model = TaskResponse , status_code = 201 ) def create_task ( task : TaskCreate , db : Session = Depends ( get_db )): db_task = Task ( title = task . title ) db . add ( db_task ) db . commit () db . refresh ( db_task ) return _task_to_dict ( db_task ) @app . patch ( '/tasks/ {task_id} /complete' , response_model = TaskResponse ) def complete_task ( task_id : int , db : Session = Depends ( get_db )): task = db . query ( Task ) . filter ( Task . id == task_id ) . first () if not task : raise HTTPException ( status_code = 404 , detail = 'Task not found' ) task . completed = True db . commit () db . refresh ( task ) return _task_to_dict ( task ) Running with the Database cd taskapi/ uvicorn app.main:app --reload tasks.db is created in the taskapi/ directory the first time the app starts. Restart the server — your tasks are still there. Inspecting the Database Directly sqlite3 tasks.db sqlite> .tables tasks sqlite> SELECT * FROM tasks ; 1 | Buy groceries | 0 | 2026 -04-16 10 :00:00.000000 2 | Write tests | 0 | 2026 -04-16 10 :01:00.000000 sqlite> .quit Key Concept: Depends(get_db) Depends(get_db) is FastAPI's dependency injection system. For every incoming request: FastAPI calls get_db() to open a database session Passes the session to your route function as db After the response is sent, runs the finally block in get_db() to close the session This happens automatically — your route function never manages the session lifecycle. Section 5 — Docker Containers vs Virtual Machines The classic deployment problem: "It works on my machine." A virtual machine solves this by bundling a full OS. A container is lighter — it shares the host OS kernel but packages your app and all its dependencies into an isolated, reproducible unit. Virtual Machine Container Includes Full OS + app App + dependencies only Startup Minutes Seconds Size Gigabytes Megabytes Isolation Separate kernel Process-level (shared kernel) Use case Running different operating systems Packaging and deploying apps How Docker Works Dockerfile docker build docker run (instructions) ──────────────► Image ──────────────► Container (snapshot) (running instance) Dockerfile — instructions for building your image Image — an immutable snapshot (like a ZIP file of your app and its environment) Container — a running instance of an image Updated Project Structure Add Dockerfile and requirements.txt to the taskapi/ root: taskapi/ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py │ └── database.py ├── Dockerfile <-- new └── requirements.txt <-- new requirements.txt Copy into taskapi/requirements.txt : fastapi==0.111.0 uvicorn[standard]==0.29.0 sqlalchemy==2.0.30 Dockerfile This uses a multi-stage build : the builder stage installs dependencies into a virtual environment; the runtime stage copies only what is needed, producing a lean final image with no build tools. Copy into taskapi/Dockerfile : # Stage 1: Builder — install dependencies FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder WORKDIR /app RUN python -m venv /opt/venv ENV PATH = "/opt/venv/bin: $PATH " COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt # Stage 2: Runtime — lean final image, no build tools FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime WORKDIR /app COPY --from = builder /opt/venv /opt/venv COPY app/ ./app/ ENV PATH = "/opt/venv/bin: $PATH " ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED = 1 ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE = 1 # Run as a non-root user — security best practice RUN adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" appuser USER appuser EXPOSE 8000 CMD [ "uvicorn" , "app.main:app" , "--host" , "0.0.0.0" , "--port" , "8000" ] Docker Commands Run all commands from the taskapi/ directory. Build the image: docker build -t taskapi . Run a container from the image: docker run -p 8000 :8000 taskapi -p 8000:8000 maps port 8000 on your machine to port 8000 inside the container. Visit http://localhost:8000/tasks — the app is now running inside a container. Other useful Docker commands: # List running containers docker ps # View container logs docker logs <container-id> # Open a shell inside a running container docker exec -it <container-id> /bin/sh # Stop a container docker stop <container-id> # List all images docker images # Remove an image docker rmi taskapi Note: The SQLite database is created inside the container's filesystem. When the container is stopped and removed, the data is lost. Section 6 solves this with a Docker volume. Section 6 — Docker Compose What Is Docker Compose? Docker Compose lets you define and run multiple containers together using a single YAML file. Instead of running a long docker run command with flags, you describe your services in docker-compose.yml and start everything with one command. docker-compose.yml | v docker compose up --build | ├── starts container: app (your FastAPI service) └── (more services added in Section 7) docker-compose.yml — Version 1 Add this file at taskapi/docker-compose.yml : services : app : build : . ports : - "8000:8000" volumes : - ./data:/app/data environment : - DATABASE_URL=sqlite:////app/data/tasks.db What each field does: Field Purpose build: . Build the image from the Dockerfile in the current directory ports Map host port 8000 to container port 8000 volumes Mount ./data on your machine to /app/data inside the container — the database file survives container restarts environment Set DATABASE_URL so the app writes tasks.db into the mounted volume The four slashes in sqlite:////app/data/tasks.db are correct: sqlite:// (scheme) + //app/data/tasks.db (absolute path). Docker Compose Commands # Build images and start all services (runs in foreground) docker compose up --build # Run in the background docker compose up --build -d # View logs docker compose logs -f # Stop and remove containers docker compose down # Stop and also remove named volumes docker compose down -v Visit http://localhost:8000/tasks — same app, now with a persistent database. Section 7 — Nginx as Reverse Proxy What Is a Reverse Proxy? A reverse proxy is a server that sits in front of your application and forwards incoming requests to it. Without Nginx: Browser ──► FastAPI :8000 With Nginx: Browser ──► Nginx :80 ──► FastAPI :8000 (internal) Why add this layer? Benefit Explanation Standard port Users connect on port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS) instead of :8000 SSL termination Nginx handles HTTPS; your app only ever sees plain HTTP internally Static files Nginx serves static files (images, CSS) directly without hitting Python Load balancing Nginx can distribute traffic across multiple app instances For this course, we use Nginx purely as a reverse proxy on port 80. Updated Project Structure taskapi/ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py │ └── database.py ├── nginx/ │ └── nginx.conf <-- new ├── Dockerfile ├── docker-compose.yml <-- updated └── requirements.txt nginx.conf Copy into taskapi/nginx/nginx.conf : upstream taskapi { server app : 8000 ; } server { listen 80 ; location / { proxy_pass http://taskapi ; proxy_set_header Host $host ; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr ; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for ; } } Key parts explained: Directive Meaning upstream taskapi Names the group of app servers to proxy to. app is the Docker Compose service name — Docker's internal DNS resolves it to the container's IP. listen 80 Accept connections on port 80 proxy_pass http://taskapi Forward all requests to the upstream group proxy_set_header Pass the original client IP and host to the app so it can log them docker-compose.yml — Version 2 Replace taskapi/docker-compose.yml with this version, which adds the nginx service: services : app : build : . expose : - "8000" volumes : - ./data:/app/data environment : - DATABASE_URL=sqlite:////app/data/tasks.db nginx : image : nginx:alpine ports : - "80:80" volumes : - ./nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf depends_on : - app What changed from version 1: Change Reason ports → expose on app The app is no longer directly reachable from outside; only Nginx talks to it Added nginx service Runs the official nginx:alpine image ports: 80:80 on nginx Only Nginx is exposed to the outside world depends_on: app Docker Compose starts app before starting nginx Testing Through Nginx docker compose up --build # Nginx is now on port 80 — no port number needed curl http://localhost/tasks curl -X POST http://localhost/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Test through Nginx"}' Section 8 — Putting It All Together Final Project Structure taskapi/ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py # FastAPI routes, Pydantic models │ └── database.py # SQLAlchemy engine, session, ORM model ├── nginx/ │ └── nginx.conf # Reverse proxy config ├── data/ # Created automatically; holds tasks.db ├── Dockerfile # Multi-stage build for the FastAPI app ├── docker-compose.yml # Orchestrates app + nginx └── requirements.txt # Python dependencies Starting the Full Stack From Scratch cd taskapi/ # Build images and start both services docker compose up --build That's it. Docker Compose builds the FastAPI image, pulls the Nginx image, creates the network, mounts volumes, and starts both containers. Request Trace: What Happens When You Call curl http://localhost/tasks 1. curl sends: GET /tasks HTTP/1.1 to 127.0.0.1:80 2. Nginx receives the request on port 80 Reads nginx.conf: location / → proxy_pass http://taskapi Forwards: GET /tasks HTTP/1.1 to app:8000 (Docker internal DNS) 3. FastAPI (uvicorn) receives the request on port 8000 Matches route: @app.get('/tasks') Opens a SQLAlchemy session via Depends(get_db) Queries: SELECT * FROM tasks Returns JSON response with status 200 4. Nginx receives the JSON response from FastAPI Forwards it back to curl unchanged 5. curl prints the JSON Component Responsibilities Summary Question Answer Who accepts the public connection? Nginx Who runs the Python code? uvicorn (inside the FastAPI container) Who validates the request body? FastAPI + Pydantic Who talks to the database? SQLAlchemy (inside the FastAPI container) Who persists data across restarts? Docker volume mounted to ./data Who wires everything together? Docker Compose Section 9 — DNS & Domain Names What Is DNS? Every server on the internet has an IP address — a numeric identifier like 203.0.113.42 . DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's naming system: it translates human-readable domain names like tasks.example.com into IP addresses that computers can connect to. Without DNS, you would need to type http://203.0.113.42/tasks instead of http://tasks.example.com/tasks . How DNS Resolution Works When you type tasks.example.com into a browser, this happens: Browser | | 1. Check browser cache (visited recently?) v Operating System | | 2. Check OS cache / /etc/hosts v Recursive Resolver (provided by your ISP or 8.8.8.8) | | 3. Ask: who handles .com? v Root Name Server | | 4. Returns: TLD server for .com v TLD Name Server (.com) | | 5. Returns: authoritative NS for example.com v Authoritative Name Server (your DNS provider) | | 6. Returns: tasks.example.com → 203.0.113.42 v Browser connects to 203.0.113.42:80 The result is cached at each level so this lookup only happens once (until the TTL expires). A Records An A record (Address record) maps a hostname to an IPv4 address. It is the most fundamental DNS record type. Type Name Value TTL A tasks.example.com 203.0.113.42 3600 A www.example.com 203.0.113.42 3600 A example.com 203.0.113.42 3600 TTL (Time To Live) is how long resolvers cache this record, in seconds. 3600 = 1 hour. Lower TTL means faster propagation of changes; higher TTL means fewer DNS lookups. Other Common Record Types Type Purpose Example A Maps hostname → IPv4 address tasks.example.com → 203.0.113.42 AAAA Maps hostname → IPv6 address tasks.example.com → 2001:db8::1 CNAME Alias — maps hostname → another hostname www.example.com → example.com MX Mail server for a domain example.com → mail.example.com TXT Arbitrary text (used for domain verification, SPF) "v=spf1 include:..." DNS Zone File (What It Looks Like) A DNS zone file is the authoritative record for a domain. Most DNS providers hide this behind a GUI, but the underlying format looks like this: ; Zone file for example.com $TTL 3600 @ IN A 203.0.113.42 ; example.com → server IP www IN A 203.0.113.42 ; www.example.com → server IP tasks IN A 203.0.113.42 ; tasks.example.com → server IP Pointing a Domain to Your Server: Step by Step Buy a domain from a registrar (Namecheap, GoDaddy, Google Domains, etc.) Find your server's IP address — this is the public IP of the machine running Docker Log in to your DNS provider (often the same as your registrar, or Cloudflare) Add an A record: Name: tasks (or @ for the root domain) Type: A Value: 203.0.113.42 (your server's IP) TTL: 3600 Wait for propagation — changes typically take 1–30 minutes (up to 48 hours if old records were cached with high TTLs) How This Connects to Our Stack Once DNS is configured: Browser types: http://tasks.example.com | | DNS resolves tasks.example.com → 203.0.113.42 v Your server at 203.0.113.42 | | port 80 v [ Nginx ] <-- receives the request | v [ FastAPI ] <-- processes it | v [ SQLite ] <-- queries the database Nginx is what listens on port 80. The moment DNS resolves your domain name to the server IP, real HTTP traffic starts flowing through the exact stack you built in this notebook. HTTPS: For production, you would configure Nginx to also listen on port 443 and obtain an SSL certificate (e.g., via Let's Encrypt / Certbot). That adds TLS termination at the Nginx layer — the rest of the stack remains unchanged. Section 10 — Challenge Extend the Task Manager API with a delete endpoint . Requirements Add DELETE /tasks/{id} to app/main.py Return 204 No Content on success (no response body) Return 404 Not Found if the task does not exist Rebuild the Docker image and bring the stack back up Verify with curl : # Create a task curl -X POST http://localhost/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Delete me"}' # Delete task 1 curl -X DELETE http://localhost/tasks/1 # Confirm it is gone curl http://localhost/tasks Solution Add this route to `app/main.py`: @app . delete ( '/tasks/ {task_id} ' , status_code = 204 ) def delete_task ( task_id : int , db : Session = Depends ( get_db )): task = db . query ( Task ) . filter ( Task . id == task_id ) . first () if not task : raise HTTPException ( status_code = 404 , detail = 'Task not found' ) db . delete ( task ) db . commit () Rebuild and restart: docker compose up --build Summary Concept Key Takeaway REST / HTTP Standard methods + status codes + JSON form the language of web APIs FastAPI Type hints + Pydantic give you validation and docs for free SQLAlchemy Maps Python classes to database tables; Depends(get_db) manages sessions Docker Packages your app and its environment into a portable, reproducible image Docker Compose One YAML file orchestrates multiple containers with correct wiring Nginx Sits in front of your app; handles port 80, connection management, and later SSL DNS / A records Maps a human domain name to your server's IP address Further Reading FastAPI documentation SQLAlchemy ORM tutorial Docker getting started guide Nginx reverse proxy guide 12-Factor App — principles behind production-grade applications

docs.text: We will build a REST API for managing tasks. Every section adds one layer to this same application until the full stack is running. Method Path Action GET /tasks List all tasks POST /tasks Create a new task PATCH /tasks/{id}/complete Mark a task as completed
docs.title: The Running Example: Task Manager API

docs.text: An API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined way for one program to communicate with another. A web API uses the HTTP protocol — the same protocol your browser uses to load web pages — as the communication channel. When you open https://weather.com , your browser sends an HTTP request and receives an HTML page. When your Python code calls a weather API, it sends the same kind of HTTP request and receives JSON. The protocol is identical; only the response format differs.
docs.title: What Is an API?

docs.text: REST (Representational State Transfer) is a set of conventions for designing web APIs: Resources are identified by URLs ( /tasks , /tasks/42 ) The HTTP method expresses what action to take Responses use standard status codes to communicate the outcome Data is exchanged as JSON An API that follows these conventions is called RESTful .
docs.title: What Is REST?

docs.text: Method Meaning Typical use GET Retrieve a resource List tasks, get one task POST Create a new resource Add a task PUT Replace a resource entirely Replace all task fields PATCH Update part of a resource Mark a task complete DELETE Remove a resource Delete a task
docs.title: HTTP Methods

docs.text: Code Meaning When it happens 200 OK Success GET returned data 201 Created Resource created POST succeeded 204 No Content Success, no response body DELETE succeeded 400 Bad Request Client sent invalid data Missing required field 404 Not Found Resource doesn't exist Task ID not in database 422 Unprocessable Entity Validation failed Wrong data type in body 500 Internal Server Error Server crashed Bug in your code Rule of thumb: 2xx = success, 4xx = the client's fault, 5xx = the server's fault.
docs.title: HTTP Status Codes

docs.text: REQUEST -------- POST /tasks HTTP/1.1 Host: localhost:8000 Content-Type: application/json {"title": "Buy groceries"} RESPONSE -------- HTTP/1.1 201 Created Content-Type: application/json {"id": 1, "title": "Buy groceries", "completed": false, "created_at": "2026-04-16T10:00:00"} Every HTTP interaction follows this shape: method + URL + headers + optional body going out, status code + headers + optional body coming back.
docs.title: Anatomy of an HTTP Request and Response

docs.text: A client is anything that sends HTTP requests to an API. The API doesn't know or care what type of client is calling it — it only sees an HTTP request. Client Typical use Web browser (via JavaScript) Loads a web app; fetch() calls the API curl Terminal tool for testing APIs manually Postman GUI tool for building and testing requests Python requests / httpx API calls from scripts and services Mobile app iOS/Android apps calling a backend Another server Microservices calling each other
docs.title: What Is a Client?

docs.text: When a web page needs data, JavaScript uses the fetch API: // JavaScript running in the browser const response = await fetch ( 'http://localhost:8000/tasks' ); const tasks = await response . json (); console . log ( tasks ); // [{"id": 1, "title": "Buy groceries", "completed": false, ...}] The browser sends an HTTP GET to your FastAPI server and receives JSON. Your Python code never knows whether the caller is a browser, a mobile app, or curl .
docs.title: How a Browser Consumes an API

docs.text: curl is the fastest way to test an API from the terminal: # List all tasks curl http://localhost:8000/tasks # Create a new task curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Buy groceries"}' # Mark task 1 as completed curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/tasks/1/complete
docs.title: Testing with curl

docs.text: FastAPI automatically generates interactive API documentation at /docs . You can send real HTTP requests directly from the browser — no curl or Postman required. Once you start the server in Section 3, visit: http://localhost:8000/docs
docs.title: FastAPI's Built-in Client: Swagger UI

docs.text: FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for building APIs. Key properties: Automatic validation — uses Python type hints and Pydantic to validate all incoming data; returns a 422 with a clear message if the data is wrong Auto-generated docs — Swagger UI at /docs with zero extra code Dependency injection — clean way to share database sessions, auth, and other resources across routes Fast — one of the fastest Python frameworks, powered by Starlette and uvicorn
docs.title: What Is FastAPI?

docs.text: Create this directory structure: taskapi/ ├── app/ │ └── main.py └── requirements.txt
docs.title: Project Structure

docs.text: Copy the code below into taskapi/app/main.py . This version stores tasks in a Python list. There is no database yet — restart the server and all tasks disappear. Section 4 fixes this. # taskapi/app/main.py (version 1 — in-memory storage) from fastapi import FastAPI , HTTPException from pydantic import BaseModel from datetime import datetime , timezone app = FastAPI ( title = 'Task Manager API' ) # In-memory storage — replaced with SQLite in Section 4 tasks = [] _next_id = 1 class TaskCreate ( BaseModel ): title : str class TaskResponse ( BaseModel ): id : int title : str completed : bool created_at : str @app . get ( '/tasks' , response_model = list [ TaskResponse ]) def list_tasks (): return tasks @app . post ( '/tasks' , response_model = TaskResponse , status_code = 201 ) def create_task ( task : TaskCreate ): global _next_id new_task = { 'id' : _next_id , 'title' : task . title , 'completed' : False , 'created_at' : datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) . isoformat (), } tasks . append ( new_task ) _next_id += 1 return new_task @app . patch ( '/tasks/ {task_id} /complete' , response_model = TaskResponse ) def complete_task ( task_id : int ): for task in tasks : if task [ 'id' ] == task_id : task [ 'completed' ] = True return task raise HTTPException ( status_code = 404 , detail = 'Task not found' )
docs.title: Version 1: In-Memory Task List

docs.text: From the taskapi/ directory: uvicorn app.main:app --reload --reload restarts the server automatically when you save a file. Visit: http://localhost:8000/tasks — the raw JSON endpoint http://localhost:8000/docs — Swagger UI (try the endpoints interactively)

docs.text: # Create two tasks curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Buy groceries"}' curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title": "Write tests"}' # List all tasks curl http://localhost:8000/tasks # Complete task 1 curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8000/tasks/1/complete
