docs.text: Send a bad request — omit the required title field: curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/tasks \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{}' FastAPI returns 422 Unprocessable Entity with a detailed error — no extra validation code needed: { "detail" : [{ "loc" : [ "body" , "title" ], "msg" : "field required" , "type" : "value_error.missing" }] } Note: Restart the server and all tasks are gone — the list lives only in memory. Section 4 adds a real database.
docs.title: How FastAPI Handles Validation

docs.text: SQLite is a file-based SQL database. The entire database is a single .db file — no separate server process, no configuration. Property SQLite Storage One file ( tasks.db ) Setup None — works out of the box Suitable for Development, small-to-medium production apps, embedded systems Not suitable for High-concurrency write-heavy workloads SQLite is the right choice for this course project and for most applications that do not need horizontal scaling.
docs.title: What Is SQLite?

docs.text: SQLAlchemy is Python's most widely used ORM (Object-Relational Mapper). It lets you define database tables as Python classes and write queries in Python rather than raw SQL. Python class ──────────► database table class Task maps to CREATE TABLE tasks (...) Python object ──────────► database row task = Task(...) maps to INSERT INTO tasks ...
docs.title: SQLAlchemy

docs.text: Add database.py alongside main.py : taskapi/ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py <-- updated (connects to database) │ └── database.py <-- new (engine, session, ORM model) └── requirements.txt Copy database.py below into taskapi/app/database.py : # taskapi/app/database.py import os from sqlalchemy import create_engine , Column , Integer , String , Boolean , DateTime from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declarative_base from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker from datetime import datetime DATABASE_URL = os . getenv ( 'DATABASE_URL' , 'sqlite:///./tasks.db' ) engine = create_engine ( DATABASE_URL , connect_args = { 'check_same_thread' : False }) SessionLocal = sessionmaker ( autocommit = False , autoflush = False , bind = engine ) Base = declarative_base () class Task ( Base ): __tablename__ = 'tasks' id = Column ( Integer , primary_key = True , index = True ) title = Column ( String , nullable = False ) completed = Column ( Boolean , default = False ) created_at = Column ( DateTime , default = datetime . utcnow ) def get_db (): """Yield a database session; close it when the request is done.""" db = SessionLocal () try : yield db finally : db . close () def create_tables (): """Create all tables if they do not already exist.""" Base . metadata . create_all ( bind = engine ) Now replace taskapi/app/main.py with the version below. The three routes are identical — only the storage layer changes from a Python list to SQLAlchemy queries. # taskapi/app/main.py (version 2 — SQLite backend) from fastapi import FastAPI , HTTPException , Depends from pydantic import BaseModel from sqlalchemy.orm import Session from app.database import Task , get_db , create_tables app = FastAPI ( title = 'Task Manager API' ) create_tables () # creates tasks.db and the tasks table on first run class TaskCreate ( BaseModel ): title : str class TaskResponse ( BaseModel ): id : int title : str completed : bool created_at : str def _task_to_dict ( task : Task ) -> dict : return { 'id' : task . id , 'title' : task . title , 'completed' : task . completed , 'created_at' : task . created_at . isoformat (), } @app . get ( '/tasks' , response_model = list [ TaskResponse ]) def list_tasks ( db : Session = Depends ( get_db )): return [ _task_to_dict ( t ) for t in db . query ( Task ) . all ()] @app . post ( '/tasks' , response_model = TaskResponse , status_code = 201 ) def create_task ( task : TaskCreate , db : Session = Depends ( get_db )): db_task = Task ( title = task . title ) db . add ( db_task ) db . commit () db . refresh ( db_task ) return _task_to_dict ( db_task ) @app . patch ( '/tasks/ {task_id} /complete' , response_model = TaskResponse ) def complete_task ( task_id : int , db : Session = Depends ( get_db )): task = db . query ( Task ) . filter ( Task . id == task_id ) . first () if not task : raise HTTPException ( status_code = 404 , detail = 'Task not found' ) task . completed = True db . commit () db . refresh ( task ) return _task_to_dict ( task )

docs.title: Running with the Database

docs.text: sqlite3 tasks.db sqlite> .tables tasks sqlite> SELECT * FROM tasks ; 1 | Buy groceries | 0 | 2026 -04-16 10 :00:00.000000 2 | Write tests | 0 | 2026 -04-16 10 :01:00.000000 sqlite> .quit

docs.text: Depends(get_db) is FastAPI's dependency injection system. For every incoming request: FastAPI calls get_db() to open a database session Passes the session to your route function as db After the response is sent, runs the finally block in get_db() to close the session This happens automatically — your route function never manages the session lifecycle.
docs.title: Key Concept: Depends(get_db)

docs.text: The classic deployment problem: "It works on my machine." A virtual machine solves this by bundling a full OS. A container is lighter — it shares the host OS kernel but packages your app and all its dependencies into an isolated, reproducible unit. Virtual Machine Container Includes Full OS + app App + dependencies only Startup Minutes Seconds Size Gigabytes Megabytes Isolation Separate kernel Process-level (shared kernel) Use case Running different operating systems Packaging and deploying apps
docs.title: Containers vs Virtual Machines

docs.text: Dockerfile docker build docker run (instructions) ──────────────► Image ──────────────► Container (snapshot) (running instance) Dockerfile — instructions for building your image Image — an immutable snapshot (like a ZIP file of your app and its environment) Container — a running instance of an image
docs.title: How Docker Works

docs.text: Add Dockerfile and requirements.txt to the taskapi/ root: taskapi/ ├── app/ │ ├── main.py │ └── database.py ├── Dockerfile <-- new └── requirements.txt <-- new

docs.title: requirements.txt

docs.text: This uses a multi-stage build : the builder stage installs dependencies into a virtual environment; the runtime stage copies only what is needed, producing a lean final image with no build tools. Copy into taskapi/Dockerfile : # Stage 1: Builder — install dependencies FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder WORKDIR /app RUN python -m venv /opt/venv ENV PATH = "/opt/venv/bin: $PATH " COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt # Stage 2: Runtime — lean final image, no build tools FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime WORKDIR /app COPY --from = builder /opt/venv /opt/venv COPY app/ ./app/ ENV PATH = "/opt/venv/bin: $PATH " ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED = 1 ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE = 1 # Run as a non-root user — security best practice RUN adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" appuser USER appuser EXPOSE 8000 CMD [ "uvicorn" , "app.main:app" , "--host" , "0.0.0.0" , "--port" , "8000" ]
docs.title: Dockerfile

docs.text: Run all commands from the taskapi/ directory. Build the image: docker build -t taskapi . Run a container from the image: docker run -p 8000 :8000 taskapi -p 8000:8000 maps port 8000 on your machine to port 8000 inside the container. Visit http://localhost:8000/tasks — the app is now running inside a container. Other useful Docker commands: # List running containers docker ps # View container logs docker logs <container-id> # Open a shell inside a running container docker exec -it <container-id> /bin/sh # Stop a container docker stop <container-id> # List all images docker images # Remove an image docker rmi taskapi Note: The SQLite database is created inside the container's filesystem. When the container is stopped and removed, the data is lost. Section 6 solves this with a Docker volume.
docs.title: Docker Commands

docs.text: Docker Compose lets you define and run multiple containers together using a single YAML file. Instead of running a long docker run command with flags, you describe your services in docker-compose.yml and start everything with one command. docker-compose.yml | v docker compose up --build | ├── starts container: app (your FastAPI service) └── (more services added in Section 7)
docs.title: What Is Docker Compose?

docs.text: Add this file at taskapi/docker-compose.yml : services : app : build : . ports : - "8000:8000" volumes : - ./data:/app/data environment : - DATABASE_URL=sqlite:////app/data/tasks.db What each field does: Field Purpose build: . Build the image from the Dockerfile in the current directory ports Map host port 8000 to container port 8000 volumes Mount ./data on your machine to /app/data inside the container — the database file survives container restarts environment Set DATABASE_URL so the app writes tasks.db into the mounted volume The four slashes in sqlite:////app/data/tasks.db are correct: sqlite:// (scheme) + //app/data/tasks.db (absolute path).

docs.text: # Build images and start all services (runs in foreground) docker compose up --build # Run in the background docker compose up --build -d # View logs docker compose logs -f # Stop and remove containers docker compose down # Stop and also remove named volumes docker compose down -v Visit http://localhost:8000/tasks — same app, now with a persistent database.

docs.text: A reverse proxy is a server that sits in front of your application and forwards incoming requests to it. Without Nginx: Browser ──► FastAPI :8000 With Nginx: Browser ──► Nginx :80 ──► FastAPI :8000 (internal) Why add this layer? Benefit Explanation Standard port Users connect on port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS) instead of :8000 SSL termination Nginx handles HTTPS; your app only ever sees plain HTTP internally Static files Nginx serves static files (images, CSS) directly without hitting Python Load balancing Nginx can distribute traffic across multiple app instances For this course, we use Nginx purely as a reverse proxy on port 80.
docs.title: What Is a Reverse Proxy?

docs.text: Copy into taskapi/nginx/nginx.conf : upstream taskapi { server app : 8000 ; } server { listen 80 ; location / { proxy_pass http://taskapi ; proxy_set_header Host $host ; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr ; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for ; } } Key parts explained: Directive Meaning upstream taskapi Names the group of app servers to proxy to. app is the Docker Compose service name — Docker's internal DNS resolves it to the container's IP. listen 80 Accept connections on port 80 proxy_pass http://taskapi Forward all requests to the upstream group proxy_set_header Pass the original client IP and host to the app so it can log them

Nginx receives the request on port 80 Reads nginx.conf: location / → proxy_pass http://taskapi Forwards: GET /tasks HTTP/1.1 to app:8000 (Docker internal DNS) 3. FastAPI (uvicorn) receives the request on port 8000 Matches route: @app.get('/tasks') Opens a SQLAlchemy session via Depends(get_db) Queries: SELECT * FROM tasks Returns JSON response with status 200 4. Nginx receives the JSON response from FastAPI Forwards it back to curl unchanged 5. curl prints the JSON

docs.text: Every server on the internet has an IP address — a numeric identifier like 203.0.113.42 . DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's naming system: it translates human-readable domain names like tasks.example.com into IP addresses that computers can connect to. Without DNS, you would need to type http://203.0.113.42/tasks instead of http://tasks.example.com/tasks .
docs.title: What Is DNS?

docs.text: When you type tasks.example.com into a browser, this happens: Browser | | 1. Check browser cache (visited recently?) v Operating System | | 2. Check OS cache / /etc/hosts v Recursive Resolver (provided by your ISP or 8.8.8.8) | | 3. Ask: who handles .com? v Root Name Server | | 4. Returns: TLD server for .com v TLD Name Server (.com) | | 5. Returns: authoritative NS for example.com v Authoritative Name Server (your DNS provider) | | 6. Returns: tasks.example.com → 203.0.113.42 v Browser connects to 203.0.113.42:80 The result is cached at each level so this lookup only happens once (until the TTL expires).
docs.title: How DNS Resolution Works

docs.text: An A record (Address record) maps a hostname to an IPv4 address. It is the most fundamental DNS record type. Type Name Value TTL A tasks.example.com 203.0.113.42 3600 A www.example.com 203.0.113.42 3600 A example.com 203.0.113.42 3600 TTL (Time To Live) is how long resolvers cache this record, in seconds. 3600 = 1 hour. Lower TTL means faster propagation of changes; higher TTL means fewer DNS lookups.
docs.title: A Records

docs.text: Type Purpose Example A Maps hostname → IPv4 address tasks.example.com → 203.0.113.42 AAAA Maps hostname → IPv6 address tasks.example.com → 2001:db8::1 CNAME Alias — maps hostname → another hostname www.example.com → example.com MX Mail server for a domain example.com → mail.example.com TXT Arbitrary text (used for domain verification, SPF) "v=spf1 include:..."
docs.title: Other Common Record Types

docs.text: A DNS zone file is the authoritative record for a domain. Most DNS providers hide this behind a GUI, but the underlying format looks like this: ; Zone file for example.com $TTL 3600 @ IN A 203.0.113.42 ; example.com → server IP www IN A 203.0.113.42 ; www.example.com → server IP tasks IN A 203.0.113.42 ; tasks.example.com → server IP
docs.title: DNS Zone File (What It Looks Like)

docs.text: Buy a domain from a registrar (Namecheap, GoDaddy, Google Domains, etc.) Find your server's IP address — this is the public IP of the machine running Docker Log in to your DNS provider (often the same as your registrar, or Cloudflare) Add an A record: Name: tasks (or @ for the root domain) Type: A Value: 203.0.113.42 (your server's IP) TTL: 3600 Wait for propagation — changes typically take 1–30 minutes (up to 48 hours if old records were cached with high TTLs)
docs.title: Pointing a Domain to Your Server: Step by Step

docs.text: Once DNS is configured: Browser types: http://tasks.example.com | | DNS resolves tasks.example.com → 203.0.113.42 v Your server at 203.0.113.42 | | port 80 v [ Nginx ] <-- receives the request | v [ FastAPI ] <-- processes it | v [ SQLite ] <-- queries the database Nginx is what listens on port 80. The moment DNS resolves your domain name to the server IP, real HTTP traffic starts flowing through the exact stack you built in this notebook. HTTPS: For production, you would configure Nginx to also listen on port 443 and obtain an SSL certificate (e.g., via Let's Encrypt / Certbot). That adds TLS termination at the Nginx layer — the rest of the stack remains unchanged.

Creating Distributable Python Packages "Namespaces are one honking great idea — let's do more of those!" — The Zen of Python Learning Objectives By the end of this notebook, you will be able to: Explain the difference between a Python script, a module, and a distributable package Structure a package using the modern src/ layout Write a complete pyproject.toml with metadata, dependencies, and build config Install your package locally in editable mode with pip install -e . Create CLI entry points so users can run your package from the terminal Build a distributable wheel ( .whl ) and source distribution ( .tar.gz ) Publish a package to TestPyPI Apply semantic versioning correctly Prerequisites Python 3.8+ installed Comfortable with functions, modules, and import Basic terminal usage (running commands) pip and build installed ( pip install build ) Section 1 — Why Not Just Share a .py File? Imagine you wrote a brilliant Python utility. You want your teammate — or the world — to use it. Your first instinct might be: "I'll just email them the file." Here's what happens next: Problem Consequence They put the file in the wrong directory ImportError — it can't be found Your code depends on requests They don't know they need to install it You fix a bug They're still using the old file They want a CLI command They have to figure out how to run the script You release v2 Nobody knows which version they have A distributable package solves all of this. It is a bundle that: Can be installed with a single command: pip install texttools Declares its own dependencies automatically Has a version number Can expose CLI commands Can be updated cleanly The Packaging Ecosystem at a Glance You write code | v [ pyproject.toml ] <- describes your package (name, version, deps...) | v [ python -m build ] <- packages your code into a distributable format | v [ .whl file ] <- the "wheel" - what pip installs | v [ pip upload to PyPI ] <- published for anyone to install | v [ pip install texttools ] <- your users install it We will build every step of this chain today. Section 2 — Anatomy of a Modern Python Package The src/ Layout There are two common ways to lay out a Python package. We will use the src/ layout — the modern, recommended approach: texttools/ <- project root (repo root) | +-- src/ | +-- texttools/ <- the actual Python package | +-- __init__.py <- makes it a package, exposes public API | +-- core.py <- core utility functions | +-- cli.py <- command-line interface | +-- tests/ | +-- test_core.py <- unit tests | +-- pyproject.toml <- package metadata and build config +-- README.md Why src/ ? Without it, Python can accidentally import your local folder instead of the installed package. The src/ directory forces Python to only use the installed version during testing. Layout Risk Flat (no src/ ) Local folder shadows installed package during tests src/ layout Tests always run against the installed package What __init__.py Does The __init__.py file serves two purposes: Signals to Python that this directory is a package (not just a folder) Defines the public API — what users see when they import texttools # src/texttools/__init__.py __version__ = "0.1.0" from texttools.core import word_count , reverse_words , title_case_smart __all__ = [ "word_count" , "reverse_words" , "title_case_smart" ] __version__ is the conventional way to expose your package version in code. __all__ controls what from texttools import * exports. Defining it makes your public API explicit. Building texttools — Step 1: Create the File Structure Let's build our package from scratch. Run the cells below in sequence. import os import pathlib # Build the package inside a temporary working directory # so it does not interfere with this notebook environment. BASE = pathlib . Path ( "texttools_project" ) dirs = [ BASE / "src" / "texttools" , BASE / "tests" , ] for d in dirs : d . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) print ( "Directories created:" ) for d in dirs : print ( f " { d } " ) Directories created: texttools_project/src/texttools texttools_project/tests # src/texttools/core.py - the actual utility functions core_code = " """ Core text utility functions for texttools. """


 def word_count(text: str) -> dict: 
 """ Count the frequency of each word in a string. 

 Args: 
 text: The input string to analyse. 

 Returns: 
 A dictionary mapping each word (lowercased) to its count. 

 Example: 
 >>> word_count( " the cat sat on the mat " ) 
 {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1} 
 """
 words = text.lower().split() 
 counts: dict = {} 
 for word in words: 
 # Strip basic punctuation 
 word = word.strip( " .,!?;:' " ) 
 if word: 
 counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1 
 return counts 


 def reverse_words(text: str) -> str: 
 """ Reverse the order of words in a string. 

 Args: 
 text: The input string. 

 Returns: 
 A new string with word order reversed. 

 Example: 
 >>> reverse_words( " Hello World " ) 
 'World Hello' 
 """
 return " " .join(reversed(text.split())) 


 def title_case_smart(text: str) -> str: 
 """ Convert a string to title case, skipping common short words. 

 Short connector words (a, an, the, and, but, or, for, nor, on, 
 at, to, by, in, of, up) remain lowercase unless they are the 
 first or last word. 

 Args: 
 text: The input string. 

 Returns: 
 A title-cased string respecting common style guidelines. 

 Example: 
 >>> title_case_smart( " the lord of the rings " ) 
 'The Lord of the Rings' 
 """
 SKIP = { " a " , " an " , " the " , " and " , " but " , " or " , " for " , " nor " , 
 " on " , " at " , " to " , " by " , " in " , " of " , " up " } 
 words = text.lower().split() 
 result = [] 
 for i, word in enumerate(words): 
 if i == 0 or i == len(words) - 1 or word not in SKIP: 
 result.append(word.capitalize()) 
 else: 
 result.append(word) 
 return " " .join(result) 
 " ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "core.py" ) . write_text ( core_code ) print ( "core.py written." ) core.py written. # src/texttools/__init__.py - the public API init_code = " """ texttools - a small text utility library. """

 __version__ = " 0.1.0 "

 from texttools.core import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart 

 __all__ = [ " word_count " , " reverse_words " , " title_case_smart " ] 
 " ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "__init__.py" ) . write_text ( init_code ) print ( "__init__.py written." ) __init__.py written. Section 3 — pyproject.toml Deep Dive pyproject.toml is the single source of truth for your package. It replaced the older setup.py and setup.cfg approach. It has three main sections: [build-system] Tells pip how to build your package. We use setuptools : [build-system] requires = [ "setuptools>=42" , "wheel" ] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] Describes what your package is: [project] name = "texttools" version = "0.1.0" description = "A small text utility library" authors = [{ name = "Your Name" , email = "you@example.com" }] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.8" license = { text = "MIT" } dependencies = [] classifiers = [ "Programming Language :: Python :: 3" , "License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License" , "Operating System :: OS Independent" , ] [project.scripts] Defines CLI commands (covered in Section 5): [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" # command module function [tool.setuptools.packages.find] Tells setuptools where to find your package — critical for the src/ layout: [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = [ "src" ] # Write the pyproject.toml for texttools pyproject = "[build-system] 
 requires = [ " setuptools>=42 " , " wheel " ] 
 build-backend = " setuptools.build_meta "

 [project] 
 name = " texttools "
 version = " 0.1.0 "
 description = " A small text utility library for word analysis and formatting "
 authors = [{name = " Your Name " , email = " you@example.com " }] 
 readme = " README.md "
 requires-python = " >=3.8 "
 license = {text = " MIT " } 
 dependencies = [] 

 classifiers = [ 
 " Programming Language :: Python :: 3 " , 
 " License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License " , 
 " Operating System :: OS Independent " , 
 ] 

 [project.scripts] 
 texttools = " texttools.cli:main "

 [tool.setuptools.packages.find] 
 where = [ " src " ] 
 " ( BASE / "pyproject.toml" ) . write_text ( pyproject ) print ( "pyproject.toml written." ) pyproject.toml written. # Write a minimal README.md (referenced by pyproject.toml) readme = "# texttools 

 A small text utility library for word analysis and formatting. 

 ## Installation 

 ```bash 
 pip install texttools 
 ``` 

 ## Usage 

 ```python 
 from texttools import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart 

 print(word_count( " the cat sat on the mat " )) 
 # {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1} 

 print(reverse_words( " Hello World " )) 
 # 'World Hello' 

 print(title_case_smart( " the lord of the rings " )) 
 # 'The Lord of the Rings' 
 ``` 

 ## CLI 

 ```bash 
 texttools count " the cat sat on the mat "
 texttools reverse " Hello World "
 texttools titlecase " the lord of the rings "
 ``` 
 " ( BASE / "README.md" ) . write_text ( readme ) print ( "README.md written." ) README.md written. Section 4 — Installing Locally with pip install -e . Before publishing to PyPI, you want to use and test your package locally. The -e flag stands for editable install . Editable Install vs Regular Install Mode Command How it works Regular pip install . Copies files into site-packages — changes require reinstall Editable pip install -e . Links to your source — changes are reflected immediately Editable mode is the standard workflow during development. How It Works Under the Hood pip install -e texttools_project/ | v reads pyproject.toml | v creates a .pth file in site-packages pointing to src/ | v Python can now find 'import texttools' import subprocess , sys result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( BASE ), "--quiet" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) if result . returncode == 0 : print ( "Package installed successfully." ) else : print ( "Error:" ) print ( result . stderr ) # Make the package importable in the current kernel session # (pip editable installs use .pth files, loaded at startup, not dynamically) src_path = str ( BASE / "src" ) if src_path not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , src_path ) print ( f "Added { src_path } to sys.path" ) Package installed successfully. Added texttools_project/src to sys.path # Verify the install # Force a fresh import in case texttools was already loaded for key in list ( sys . modules . keys ()): if key . startswith ( "texttools" ): del sys . modules [ key ] import texttools print ( f "texttools version: { texttools . __version__ } " ) print () sample = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" print ( "word_count():" ) print ( texttools . word_count ( sample )) print () print ( "reverse_words():" ) print ( texttools . reverse_words ( sample )) print () print ( "title_case_smart():" ) print ( texttools . title_case_smart ( "the lord of the rings: the return of the king" )) texttools version: 0.1.0 word_count(): {'the': 2, 'quick': 1, 'brown': 1, 'fox': 1, 'jumps': 1, 'over': 1, 'lazy': 1, 'dog': 1} reverse_words(): dog lazy the over jumps fox brown quick the title_case_smart(): The Lord of the Rings: the Return of the King Section 5 — Entry Points: Creating CLI Commands Entry points let users run your package as a command from the terminal: $ texttools count "the cat sat on the mat" cat: 1 mat: 1 on: 1 sat: 1 the: 2 How It Works When pip installs your package, it reads [project.scripts] in pyproject.toml : [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" # command module function pip creates a small wrapper executable ( texttools ) in the system bin/ directory that calls texttools.cli.main() . Writing the CLI Module The cli.py module uses argparse to parse command-line arguments. # src/texttools/cli.py - command-line interface cli_code = " """ Command-line interface for texttools. """

 import argparse 
 import sys 
 from texttools.core import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart 


 def main() -> None: 
 """ Entry point for the texttools CLI. """
 parser = argparse.ArgumentParser( 
 prog= " texttools " , 
 description= " Text utility commands " , 
 ) 

 subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest= " command " , required=True) 

 # count command 
 count_parser = subparsers.add_parser( " count " , help= " Count word frequencies " ) 
 count_parser.add_argument( " text " , help= " Text to analyse " ) 

 # reverse command 
 reverse_parser = subparsers.add_parser( " reverse " , help= " Reverse word order " ) 
 reverse_parser.add_argument( " text " , help= " Text to reverse " ) 

 # titlecase command 
 title_parser = subparsers.add_parser( " titlecase " , help= " Smart title case " ) 
 title_parser.add_argument( " text " , help= " Text to convert " ) 

 args = parser.parse_args() 

 if args.command == " count " : 
 counts = word_count(args.text) 
 for word, n in sorted(counts.items()): 
 print(f " {word} : {n} " ) 

 elif args.command == " reverse " : 
 print(reverse_words(args.text)) 

 elif args.command == " titlecase " : 
 print(title_case_smart(args.text)) 


 if __name__ == " __main__ " : 
 main() 
 " ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "cli.py" ) . write_text ( cli_code ) print ( "cli.py written." ) # Reinstall to register the entry point result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( BASE ), "--quiet" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "Package reinstalled." if result . returncode == 0 else result . stderr ) # Ensure src/ stays on path if src_path not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , src_path ) cli.py written. Package reinstalled. # Test the CLI programmatically result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "texttools.cli" , "count" , "the cat sat on the mat" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "texttools count 'the cat sat on the mat':" ) print ( result . stdout ) result2 = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "texttools.cli" , "titlecase" , "the lord of the rings" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "texttools titlecase 'the lord of the rings':" ) print ( result2 . stdout ) texttools count 'the cat sat on the mat': cat: 1 mat: 1 on: 1 sat: 1 the: 2 texttools titlecase 'the lord of the rings': The Lord of the Rings Note on if __name__ == "__main__" : This guard lets you run the module directly with python -m texttools.cli . Entry points call main() directly — the guard is for manual invocation during development. Section 6 — Testing the Installed Package A critical point: tests should run against the installed package, not the local source files. This is exactly what the src/ layout guarantees. Test Structure tests/ +-- test_core.py Note: no __init__.py in tests/ . pytest does not need it, and omitting it avoids import conflicts. # Write the test file test_code = " """ Tests for texttools.core """

 import pytest 
 from texttools import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart 


 class TestWordCount: 
 def test_basic_count(self): 
 result = word_count( " the cat sat on the mat " ) 
 assert result[ " the " ] == 2 
 assert result[ " cat " ] == 1 

 def test_case_insensitive(self): 
 result = word_count( " Python python PYTHON " ) 
 assert result[ " python " ] == 3 

 def test_strips_punctuation(self): 
 result = word_count( " hello, world! " ) 
 assert " hello " in result 
 assert " world " in result 

 def test_empty_string(self): 
 assert word_count( "" ) == {} 


 class TestReverseWords: 
 def test_basic_reverse(self): 
 assert reverse_words( " Hello World " ) == " World Hello "

 def test_single_word(self): 
 assert reverse_words( " Python " ) == " Python "

 def test_multiple_words(self): 
 assert reverse_words( " one two three " ) == " three two one "


 class TestTitleCaseSmart: 
 def test_short_words_lowercase(self): 
 result = title_case_smart( " the lord of the rings " ) 
 assert result == " The Lord of the Rings "

 def test_first_word_always_capitalised(self): 
 result = title_case_smart( " of mice and men " ) 
 assert result.startswith( " Of " ) 

 def test_last_word_always_capitalised(self): 
 result = title_case_smart( " the cat in the hat " ) 
 assert result.endswith( " Hat " ) 

 def test_single_word(self): 
 assert title_case_smart( " python " ) == " Python "

Before You Publish Create an account at test.pypi.org Generate an API token: Account Settings → API Tokens Install twine : pip install twine The Workflow Build -> Validate -> Upload python -m build twine check twine upload dist/* Step 1 — Validate Before Uploading twine check verifies your metadata is well-formed and the README renders correctly on PyPI. # Install twine subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "twine" , "--quiet" ], capture_output = True ) import glob as glob_module dist_files = glob_module . glob ( str ( BASE / "dist" / "*" )) result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "twine" , "check" ] + dist_files , capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( result . stdout ) if result . stderr : print ( result . stderr ) Checking texttools_project/dist/texttools-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl: [32mPASSED[0m Checking texttools_project/dist/texttools-0.1.0.tar.gz: [32mPASSED[0m Step 2 — Upload to TestPyPI This is not auto-executed — you need a real TestPyPI account and token. # Run in your terminal twine upload --repository testpypi dist/* When prompted: - Username: __token__ (literally) - Password: your API token (starts with pypi- ) Or use a .pypirc config file: # ~/.pypirc [testpypi] username = __token__ password = pypi-your-token-here Step 3 — Install From TestPyPI pip install --index-url https://test.pypi.org/simple/ texttools Step 4 — Publish to Real PyPI twine upload dist/* pip install texttools Section 9 — Versioning Best Practices Semantic Versioning (SemVer) The standard for Python packages is SemVer : MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH 1 . 4 . 2 ^ ^ ^ MAJOR MINOR PATCH Part Increment when... Example MAJOR You break backwards compatibility 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0 MINOR You add functionality (backwards-compatible) 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0 PATCH You fix a bug (backwards-compatible) 1.0.0 -> 1.0.1 0.x.y versions (like 0.1.0 ) signal that the API is not yet stable. The Single Source of Truth Problem Version numbers appear in two places: pyproject.toml -> version = "0.1.0" src/texttools/__init__.py -> __version__ = "0.1.0" If you update one and forget the other, they diverge. Two clean solutions: Option A — Read from installed metadata at runtime (Python 3.8+): # Option A: importlib.metadata reads version from the installed package metadata. # pyproject.toml is the ONLY place you define the version. from importlib.metadata import version , PackageNotFoundError try : pkg_version = version ( "texttools" ) except PackageNotFoundError : pkg_version = "unknown" print ( f "Version from metadata: { pkg_version } " ) Version from metadata: 0.1.0 Option B — Keep __version__ in __init__.py , read it in pyproject.toml : [project] dynamic = [ "version" ] [tool.setuptools.dynamic] version = { attr = "texttools.__version__" } With this, pyproject.toml reads the version from your __init__.py — one place to change it. Bumping Versions 1. Update version in pyproject.toml (and __init__.py if applicable) 2. git commit -m "bump version to 0.2.0" 3. git tag v0.2.0 4. python -m build 5. twine upload dist/* Important: PyPI does not allow re-uploading the same version. Section 10 — Full Package Checklist Structure [ ] src/<package>/ layout with __init__.py [ ] __version__ defined (or using importlib.metadata) [ ] tests/ directory with no __init__.py [ ] README.md with installation and usage examples pyproject.toml [ ] name is unique (check PyPI first) [ ] version follows SemVer [ ] description is a single informative sentence [ ] requires-python set correctly [ ] dependencies listed (even if empty) [ ] classifiers added [ ] [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] set Quality [ ] All functions have docstrings [ ] Tests cover happy path and edge cases [ ] twine check passes with no warnings Publishing [ ] Tested on TestPyPI first [ ] Git tag created for this version [ ] No secrets or credentials in the code Challenge — Build Your Own Package Build a distributable package called numtools (or choose your own name) from scratch. Requirements Use the src/ layout Have a proper pyproject.toml with all required fields Expose at least 3 functions in its public API via __init__.py Have a CLI entry point with at least 2 subcommands Include tests covering each function Pass twine check after building Suggested Function Ideas Theme Possible Functions Numbers is_prime(n) , fibonacci(n) , factorial(n) Dates days_until(date) , is_weekend(date) , format_date(date, style) Files count_lines(path) , find_duplicates(dir) , largest_files(dir, n) Colours hex_to_rgb(hex) , rgb_to_hex(r,g,b) , contrast_ratio(c1, c2) Starter Structure numtools/ +-- src/ | +-- numtools/ | +-- __init__.py | +-- core.py | +-- cli.py +-- tests/ | +-- test_core.py +-- pyproject.toml +-- README.md # Your workspace - build numtools here challenge_base = pathlib . Path ( "numtools" ) # TODO: Create the src/numtools/ and tests/ directories # TODO: Write core.py with at least 3 functions # TODO: Write __init__.py exposing the public API # TODO: Write cli.py with a main() entry point # TODO: Write pyproject.toml # TODO: Write test_core.py # TODO: pip install -e numtools/ # TODO: pytest numtools/tests/ # TODO: python -m build numtools/ # TODO: twine check numtools/dist/* print ( "Good luck!" ) Good luck! Hint - pyproject.toml skeleton [build-system] requires = [ "setuptools>=42" , "wheel" ] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "numtools" version = "0.1.0" description = "YOUR DESCRIPTION HERE" authors = [{ name = "Your Name" , email = "you@example.com" }] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.8" license = { text = "MIT" } dependencies = [] [project.scripts] numtools = "numtools.cli:main" [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = [ "src" ] Hint - is_prime() implementation def is_prime ( n : int ) -> bool : if n < 2 : return False for i in range ( 2 , int ( n ** 0.5 ) + 1 ): if n % i == 0 : return False return True Summary Concept Key Takeaway src/ layout Prevents local source from shadowing the installed package __init__.py Defines the public API; holds __version__ pyproject.toml Single config for metadata, build system, and tooling Editable install pip install -e . — changes are live without reinstalling Entry points [project.scripts] maps a terminal command to a Python function python -m build Produces .whl and .tar.gz in dist/ twine Validates and uploads distributions to PyPI/TestPyPI SemVer MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH — be intentional about which number you bump Further Reading Python Packaging User Guide pyproject.toml specification TestPyPI setuptools documentation

docs.text: Imagine you wrote a brilliant Python utility. You want your teammate — or the world — to use it. Your first instinct might be: "I'll just email them the file." Here's what happens next: Problem Consequence They put the file in the wrong directory ImportError — it can't be found Your code depends on requests They don't know they need to install it You fix a bug They're still using the old file They want a CLI command They have to figure out how to run the script You release v2 Nobody knows which version they have A distributable package solves all of this. It is a bundle that: Can be installed with a single command: pip install texttools Declares its own dependencies automatically Has a version number Can expose CLI commands Can be updated cleanly
docs.title: Section 1 — Why Not Just Share a .py File?

docs.text: You write code | v [ pyproject.toml ] <- describes your package (name, version, deps...) | v [ python -m build ] <- packages your code into a distributable format | v [ .whl file ] <- the "wheel" - what pip installs | v [ pip upload to PyPI ] <- published for anyone to install | v [ pip install texttools ] <- your users install it We will build every step of this chain today.
docs.title: The Packaging Ecosystem at a Glance
Section 2 — Anatomy of a Modern Python Package

docs.text: There are two common ways to lay out a Python package. We will use the src/ layout — the modern, recommended approach: texttools/ <- project root (repo root) | +-- src/ | +-- texttools/ <- the actual Python package | +-- __init__.py <- makes it a package, exposes public API | +-- core.py <- core utility functions | +-- cli.py <- command-line interface | +-- tests/ | +-- test_core.py <- unit tests | +-- pyproject.toml <- package metadata and build config +-- README.md Why src/ ? Without it, Python can accidentally import your local folder instead of the installed package. The src/ directory forces Python to only use the installed version during testing. Layout Risk Flat (no src/ ) Local folder shadows installed package during tests src/ layout Tests always run against the installed package
docs.title: The src/ Layout

docs.text: The __init__.py file serves two purposes: Signals to Python that this directory is a package (not just a folder) Defines the public API — what users see when they import texttools # src/texttools/__init__.py __version__ = "0.1.0" from texttools.core import word_count , reverse_words , title_case_smart __all__ = [ "word_count" , "reverse_words" , "title_case_smart" ] __version__ is the conventional way to expose your package version in code. __all__ controls what from texttools import * exports. Defining it makes your public API explicit.
docs.title: What __init__.py Does

docs.text:
Let's build our package from scratch. Run the cells below in sequence. import os import pathlib # Build the package inside a temporary working directory # so it does not interfere with this notebook environment. BASE = pathlib . Path ( "texttools_project" ) dirs = [ BASE / "src" / "texttools" , BASE / "tests" , ] for d in dirs : d . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) print ( "Directories created:" ) for d in dirs : print ( f " { d } " ) Directories created: texttools_project/src/texttools texttools_project/tests # src/texttools/core.py - the actual utility functions core_code = " """ Core text utility functions for texttools. """


 def word_count(text: str) -> dict: 
 """ Count the frequency of each word in a string. 

 Args: 
 text: The input string to analyse. 

 Returns: 
 A dictionary mapping each word (lowercased) to its count. 

 Example: 
 >>> word_count( " the cat sat on the mat " ) 
 {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1} 
 """
 words = text.lower().split() 
 counts: dict = {} 
 for word in words: 
 # Strip basic punctuation 
 word = word.strip( " .,!?;:' " ) 
 if word: 
 counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1 
 return counts 


 def reverse_words(text: str) -> str: 
 """ Reverse the order of words in a string. 

 Args: 
 text: The input string. 

 Returns: 
 A new string with word order reversed. 

 Example: 
 >>> reverse_words( " Hello World " ) 
 'World Hello' 
 """
 return " " .join(reversed(text.split())) 


 def title_case_smart(text: str) -> str: 
 """ Convert a string to title case, skipping common short words. 

 Short connector words (a, an, the, and, but, or, for, nor, on, 
 at, to, by, in, of, up) remain lowercase unless they are the 
 first or last word. 

 Args: 
 text: The input string. 

 Returns: 
 A title-cased string respecting common style guidelines. 

 Example: 
 >>> title_case_smart( " the lord of the rings " ) 
 'The Lord of the Rings' 
 """
 SKIP = { " a " , " an " , " the " , " and " , " but " , " or " , " for " , " nor " , 
 " on " , " at " , " to " , " by " , " in " , " of " , " up " } 
 words = text.lower().split() 
 result = [] 
 for i, word in enumerate(words): 
 if i == 0 or i == len(words) - 1 or word not in SKIP: 
 result.append(word.capitalize()) 
 else: 
 result.append(word) 
 return " " .join(result) 
 " ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "core.py" ) . write_text ( core_code ) print ( "core.py written." ) core.py written. # src/texttools/__init__.py - the public API init_code = " """ texttools - a small text utility library. """

 __version__ = " 0.1.0 "

 from texttools.core import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart 

 __all__ = [ " word_count " , " reverse_words " , " title_case_smart " ] 
 " ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "__init__.py" ) . write_text ( init_code ) print ( "__init__.py written." ) __init__.py written.

docs.text: pyproject.toml is the single source of truth for your package. It replaced the older setup.py and setup.cfg approach. It has three main sections:
docs.title: Section 3 — pyproject.toml Deep Dive

docs.text: Tells pip how to build your package. We use setuptools : [build-system] requires = [ "setuptools>=42" , "wheel" ] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"
docs.title: [build-system]

docs.text: Describes what your package is: [project] name = "texttools" version = "0.1.0" description = "A small text utility library" authors = [{ name = "Your Name" , email = "you@example.com" }] readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.8" license = { text = "MIT" } dependencies = [] classifiers = [ "Programming Language :: Python :: 3" , "License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License" , "Operating System :: OS Independent" , ]
docs.title: [project]

docs.text: Defines CLI commands (covered in Section 5): [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" # command module function

docs.text:
Tells setuptools where to find your package — critical for the src/ layout: [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = [ "src" ] # Write the pyproject.toml for texttools pyproject = "[build-system] 
 requires = [ " setuptools>=42 " , " wheel " ] 
 build-backend = " setuptools.build_meta "

 [project] 
 name = " texttools "
 version = " 0.1.0 "

 authors = [{name = " Your Name " , email = " you@example.com " }] 
 readme = " README.md "

 " Programming Language :: Python :: 3 " , 
 " License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License " , 
 " Operating System :: OS Independent " , 
 ] 

 [project.scripts] 
 texttools = " texttools.cli:main "

 [tool.setuptools.packages.find] 
 where = [ " src " ] 
 " ( BASE / "pyproject.toml" ) . write_text ( pyproject ) print ( "pyproject.toml written." ) pyproject.toml written. # Write a minimal README.md (referenced by pyproject.toml) readme = "# texttools 

 A small text utility library for word analysis and formatting. 

 ## Installation 

 ```bash 
 pip install texttools 
 ``` 

 ## Usage 

 ```python 
 from texttools import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart 

 print(word_count( " the cat sat on the mat " )) 
 # {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'sat': 1, 'on': 1, 'mat': 1} 

 print(reverse_words( " Hello World " )) 
 # 'World Hello' 

 print(title_case_smart( " the lord of the rings " )) 
 # 'The Lord of the Rings' 
 ``` 

 ## CLI 

 ```bash 
 texttools count " the cat sat on the mat "
 texttools reverse " Hello World "
 texttools titlecase " the lord of the rings "
 ``` 
 " ( BASE / "README.md" ) . write_text ( readme ) print ( "README.md written." ) README.md written.

docs.text: Before publishing to PyPI, you want to use and test your package locally. The -e flag stands for editable install .
docs.title: Section 4 — Installing Locally with pip install -e .

docs.text: Mode Command How it works Regular pip install . Copies files into site-packages — changes require reinstall Editable pip install -e . Links to your source — changes are reflected immediately Editable mode is the standard workflow during development.
docs.title: Editable Install vs Regular Install

docs.text: pip install -e texttools_project/ | v reads pyproject.toml | v creates a .pth file in site-packages pointing to src/ | v Python can now find 'import texttools' import subprocess , sys result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( BASE ), "--quiet" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) if result . returncode == 0 : print ( "Package installed successfully." ) else : print ( "Error:" ) print ( result . stderr ) # Make the package importable in the current kernel session # (pip editable installs use .pth files, loaded at startup, not dynamically) src_path = str ( BASE / "src" ) if src_path not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , src_path ) print ( f "Added { src_path } to sys.path" ) Package installed successfully. Added texttools_project/src to sys.path # Verify the install # Force a fresh import in case texttools was already loaded for key in list ( sys . modules . keys ()): if key . startswith ( "texttools" ): del sys . modules [ key ] import texttools print ( f "texttools version: { texttools . __version__ } " ) print () sample = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" print ( "word_count():" ) print ( texttools . word_count ( sample )) print () print ( "reverse_words():" ) print ( texttools . reverse_words ( sample )) print () print ( "title_case_smart():" ) print ( texttools . title_case_smart ( "the lord of the rings: the return of the king" )) texttools version: 0.1.0 word_count(): {'the': 2, 'quick': 1, 'brown': 1, 'fox': 1, 'jumps': 1, 'over': 1, 'lazy': 1, 'dog': 1} reverse_words(): dog lazy the over jumps fox brown quick the title_case_smart(): The Lord of the Rings: the Return of the King
docs.title: How It Works Under the Hood

docs.text: Entry points let users run your package as a command from the terminal: $ texttools count "the cat sat on the mat" cat: 1 mat: 1 on: 1 sat: 1 the: 2
docs.title: Section 5 — Entry Points: Creating CLI Commands

docs.text: When pip installs your package, it reads [project.scripts] in pyproject.toml : [project.scripts] texttools = "texttools.cli:main" # command module function pip creates a small wrapper executable ( texttools ) in the system bin/ directory that calls texttools.cli.main() .
docs.title: How It Works

docs.text:
The cli.py module uses argparse to parse command-line arguments. # src/texttools/cli.py - command-line interface cli_code = " """ Command-line interface for texttools. """

 import argparse 
 import sys 
 from texttools.core import word_count, reverse_words, title_case_smart 


 def main() -> None: 
 """ Entry point for the texttools CLI. """
 parser = argparse.ArgumentParser( 
 prog= " texttools " , 
 description= " Text utility commands " , 
 ) 

 subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest= " command " , required=True) 

 # count command 
 count_parser = subparsers.add_parser( " count " , help= " Count word frequencies " ) 
 count_parser.add_argument( " text " , help= " Text to analyse " ) 

 # reverse command 
 reverse_parser = subparsers.add_parser( " reverse " , help= " Reverse word order " ) 
 reverse_parser.add_argument( " text " , help= " Text to reverse " ) 

 # titlecase command 
 title_parser = subparsers.add_parser( " titlecase " , help= " Smart title case " ) 
 title_parser.add_argument( " text " , help= " Text to convert " ) 

 args = parser.parse_args() 

 if args.command == " count " : 
 counts = word_count(args.text) 
 for word, n in sorted(counts.items()): 
 print(f " {word} : {n} " ) 

 elif args.command == " reverse " : 
 print(reverse_words(args.text)) 

 elif args.command == " titlecase " : 
 print(title_case_smart(args.text)) 


 if __name__ == " __main__ " : 
 main() 
 " ( BASE / "src" / "texttools" / "cli.py" ) . write_text ( cli_code ) print ( "cli.py written." ) # Reinstall to register the entry point result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-e" , str ( BASE ), "--quiet" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "Package reinstalled." if result . returncode == 0 else result . stderr ) # Ensure src/ stays on path if src_path not in sys . path : sys . path . insert ( 0 , src_path ) cli.py written. Package reinstalled. # Test the CLI programmatically result = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "texttools.cli" , "count" , "the cat sat on the mat" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "texttools count 'the cat sat on the mat':" ) print ( result . stdout ) result2 = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , "-m" , "texttools.cli" , "titlecase" , "the lord of the rings" ], capture_output = True , text = True ) print ( "texttools titlecase 'the lord of the rings':" ) print ( result2 . stdout ) texttools count 'the cat sat on the mat': cat: 1 mat: 1 on: 1 sat: 1 the: 2 texttools titlecase 'the lord of the rings': The Lord of the Rings Note on if __name__ == "__main__" : This guard lets you run the module directly with python -m texttools.cli . Entry points call main() directly — the guard is for manual invocation during development.

docs.text: A critical point: tests should run against the installed package, not the local source files. This is exactly what the src/ layout guarantees.

docs.text: The standard for Python packages is SemVer : MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH 1 . 4 . 2 ^ ^ ^ MAJOR MINOR PATCH Part Increment when... Example MAJOR You break backwards compatibility 1.0.0 -> 2.0.0 MINOR You add functionality (backwards-compatible) 1.0.0 -> 1.1.0 PATCH You fix a bug (backwards-compatible) 1.0.0 -> 1.0.1 0.x.y versions (like 0.1.0 ) signal that the API is not yet stable.
docs.title: Semantic Versioning (SemVer)

docs.text: Version numbers appear in two places: pyproject.toml -> version = "0.1.0" src/texttools/__init__.py -> __version__ = "0.1.0" If you update one and forget the other, they diverge. Two clean solutions: Option A — Read from installed metadata at runtime (Python 3.8+): # Option A: importlib.metadata reads version from the installed package metadata. # pyproject.toml is the ONLY place you define the version. from importlib.metadata import version , PackageNotFoundError try : pkg_version = version ( "texttools" ) except PackageNotFoundError : pkg_version = "unknown" print ( f "Version from metadata: { pkg_version } " ) Version from metadata: 0.1.0 Option B — Keep __version__ in __init__.py , read it in pyproject.toml : [project] dynamic = [ "version" ] [tool.setuptools.dynamic] version = { attr = "texttools.__version__" } With this, pyproject.toml reads the version from your __init__.py — one place to change it.

docs.text: 1. Update version in pyproject.toml (and __init__.py if applicable) 2. git commit -m "bump version to 0.2.0" 3. git tag v0.2.0 4. python -m build 5. twine upload dist/* Important: PyPI does not allow re-uploading the same version.
